# Shell scripts {#sec-shell-scripts}

**Core.** Work through it, with the exercises.

::: {.callout-note .goals icon=false}
## Learning goals

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Save commands as a script, run it, and read any line of one,
   including the script from @sec-organizing-projects.
2. Use variables, `$( )`, and `$(( ))`, and quote every expansion so
   file names with spaces stay whole.
3. Loop over files and over the rows of a sample table, and preview a
   loop before it changes anything.
4. Take file names as arguments, check inputs with `if` and tests, and
   explain what `set -euo pipefail` catches and what it misses.
5. Keep results and messages apart in a log, chain numbered scripts
   into a small pipeline, and save and recover script versions with
   git.
:::

## What this chapter does {#sec-shell-scripts-intro}

In Chapters 1 to 7 you typed commands one at a time and pasted the
occasional block. A **script** is those commands saved in a file. Saved,
they run the same way every time, they record exactly what was done,
and you can share them, keep their history, and, in @sec-hpc-slurm,
hand them to a cluster to run as a job. You have already run one:
@sec-organizing-projects asked you to paste `src/01_count_reads.sh` into
your project and run it on trust. By @sec-shell-scripts-read you will be
able to explain every line of it.

Several earlier chapters left loose ends here. @sec-orientation's read
count `$(( $(gunzip -c … | wc -l) / 4 ))` was copied without
explanation, and so was its warning that the shell does not stop on
errors unless told to. @sec-getting-help said that whether a script
stops after a failing command "depends on the program and the script".
@sec-text-tools promised `set -o pipefail` and said that `grep`'s exit
status 1 matters "in scripts that stop on any nonzero status".
@sec-linux-system gave you the shebang line and the `x` bit. This
chapter ties them together.

It is the longest chapter in Part II, so it comes in **two sittings**,
marked in the text:

- **A. Writing scripts** (@sec-shell-scripts-first to
  @sec-shell-scripts-arguments): saving commands in a file, variables
  and quoting, loops, tests, and arguments. Exercise 1, part A, fits at
  the end.
- **B. Making them dependable** (@sec-shell-scripts-strict to
  @sec-shell-scripts-git): stopping on errors, logging, reading
  @sec-organizing-projects's script line by line, chaining scripts into
  a small pipeline, finding bugs, and saving scripts with git.

Practice happens in a scratch folder, `~/bioinf-computing-ch08`. Make it
now, with a `bin/` folder inside for the exercise scripts:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08
```

Most examples in sitting A **read** the practice folder
`~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/` from @sec-shell-basics: the run
folders, the one with spaces in its name, the stray `.tmp` file, and
the two sample tables. Nothing in this chapter changes, renames, or
deletes anything there, so later chapters still find it as they expect.
Scripts that write files write them in `~/bioinf-computing-ch08`. If you
do not have the practice folder, paste the setup block from
@sec-shell-basics-intro first.

The project, `~/bioinf-computing`, is touched only in sitting B: you
read `src/01_count_reads.sh`, add two scripts beside it, and turn the
project into a git repository.

The outputs shown were captured on a Mac (macOS 15, Homebrew bash
5.3.15 with the GNU tools first on `PATH`, as set up in
@sec-orientation) and on Ubuntu 24.04 (bash 5.2.21), with GNU gzip. A
Mac's own `gunzip` words its errors differently (`gunzip: can't stat:
…` where GNU says `gzip: …: No such file or directory`), and so do
other versions; the meaning is the same. Paths start with `/home/you`
on Linux and `/Users/you` on a Mac.

## From the command line to a script {#sec-shell-scripts-first}

Start with a command you already know. @sec-text-tools counted the
feature types in the book's annotation file with one pipeline:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c ~/bioinf-computing/data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr
```

```{.console}
    129 exon
    124 transcript
    118 CDS
    115 start_codon
    114 stop_codon
```

Typing that again next month means remembering it exactly. Save it
instead. Open a new file in VS Code (or `nano` if you prefer, as in
@sec-book-setup):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
code ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/gtf_types.sh
```

Paste these lines and save:

```{.bash filename="~/bioinf-computing-ch08/gtf_types.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# gtf_types.sh: count the feature types (column 3) in the book's GTF file.
# Run:     bash gtf_types.sh   (from ~/bioinf-computing-ch08)
# Input:   ~/bioinf-computing/data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
# Output:  counts on the screen, most common first
gunzip -c ~/bioinf-computing/data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr
```

The first line is the shebang from @sec-linux-system-scripts. The lines
starting with `#` are **comments**: bash skips them, and they are for
the next person to read the file, who is usually you. A short header
saying what the script does, how to run it, what it reads, and what it
writes is worth the four lines in every script you keep.

Run it, first with `bash`, then as a command of its own:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08
bash gtf_types.sh
./gtf_types.sh
chmod u+x gtf_types.sh
./gtf_types.sh
```

`bash gtf_types.sh` prints the same five lines as before.
`./gtf_types.sh` then fails with `bash: ./gtf_types.sh: Permission
denied` (exit status 126) until `chmod u+x` gives the file its `x` bit,
exactly as `hello.sh` did in @sec-linux-system-scripts. After that, it
prints the five lines again.

**What a script is.** A script is a text file of commands that a **new
bash process** reads and runs from top to bottom. Because it is a new
process, it starts fresh: it does not see the aliases you typed or the
variables you set without `export` in your terminal
(@tbl-variable-lifetime). It also cannot change your terminal: a `cd`
or a variable set inside the script is gone when the script ends.

**Relative paths are read from where you run it.** A script does not
run "from its own folder". Every relative path in it is read from the
folder you are in when you start it. @sec-shell-basics left a two-line
script for exactly this, `~/bioinf-computing-ch05/where.sh`, which runs
`pwd` and then `ls data/raw`. Run it from your home folder:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~
bash ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/where.sh
```

```{.console}
/home/you
ls: cannot access 'data/raw': No such file or directory
```

The script is stored in `~/bioinf-computing-ch05`, but `pwd` says it
runs in `~`, and `data/raw` is looked up there. `gtf_types.sh` does not
have this problem because its one path starts with `~`, which is
absolute. Project scripts use relative paths on purpose, so a project
folder can be moved or copied as a whole. The book's rule is simple:
**project scripts live in `src/` and are run from the project folder**,
as `pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh`, and each says so in its
header. @sec-shell-scripts-read adds one line that checks it.

**The parts of a script.** Longer scripts follow the same order as the
header lines above, and @fig-script-anatomy shows it on
@sec-organizing-projects's script: the shebang; a header comment;
settings that change how bash behaves; the inputs and checks on them;
the work; and the outputs. You will meet each part in this chapter and
read that script line by line in @sec-shell-scripts-read.

::: {#fig-script-anatomy}
{{< svg ../figures/script-anatomy.svg >}}

The parts of a script, shown on `src/01_count_reads.sh` from
@sec-organizing-projects (shortened): the shebang line, a header
comment saying what it does and how to run it, a settings line
(`set -euo pipefail`, @sec-shell-scripts-strict), inputs and checks,
the work, and the outputs, written to a temporary name and then moved
into place, with a log of the run. @sec-shell-scripts-read uses this
map to read every line.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** You run `bash ~/bioinf-computing/src/01_count_reads.sh`
from your home folder instead of from the project folder. What goes
wrong, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
The script's paths are relative, so they are read from `~`. Its
`mkdir -p results logs` makes those two folders in your home folder,
then `md5sum` cannot find `src/01_count_reads.sh` and `cd data/raw`
fails with `No such file or directory`. Run project scripts from the
project folder; @sec-shell-scripts-read adds a guard that stops the
script straight away when you do not.
:::
:::

## Variables, quoting, and expansions {#sec-shell-scripts-variables}

Go to the practice folder and store a folder name in a **variable**,
then list that folder twice, once without quotes and once with them:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
d="Run 3 final"
ls $d
ls "$d"
```

```{.console}
ls: cannot access 'Run': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access '3': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access 'final': No such file or directory
sample_C_R1.fq.gz
sample_C_R2.fq.gz
```

The first `ls` exits with status 2 after three errors; the second lists
the two files.

**What happened.** `d="Run 3 final"` stores the text `Run 3 final`
under the name `d` (no spaces around `=`, @sec-linux-system-variables).
When bash meets `$d`, it replaces it with that value. Without quotes,
bash then does two more things to the value, the steps that
@fig-shell-steps in @sec-shell-basics set aside:

1. **Word splitting.** The value is cut at spaces, tabs, and newlines
   (the default contents of a setting called `IFS`) into separate
   words. `Run 3 final` becomes three words, so `ls` received three
   names.
2. **Wildcard matching.** Each piece that holds `*`, `?`, or `[` is
   matched against file names, as if you had typed it
   (@sec-shell-basics-wildcards).

Inside double quotes neither happens: `"$d"` is replaced by its value
and stays **one word**, spaces and all (@fig-word-splitting). That gives
the rule this chapter follows everywhere:

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
Put double quotes around every `$…`: write `"$d"`, `"$f"`, `"$1"`. An
unquoted value is split at spaces and matched as a wildcard, so a file
name with a space becomes several arguments.
:::

::: {#fig-word-splitting}
{{< svg ../figures/word-splitting.svg >}}

What bash does with `gunzip -c $f` when `f` holds `Run 3
final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz`. The variable is replaced by its value, the
unquoted value is split at its spaces into three words, and `gunzip`
receives three file names that do not exist. The last step shows
`"$f"`, which arrives as one word. Use *Next* to step through.
:::

Two places do not split, and you will see unquoted variables in them in
other people's scripts: a plain assignment (`x=$y` copies the value
whole) and the inside of `[[ … ]]` (@sec-shell-scripts-conditionals).
Quoting there does no harm, and quoting everywhere is the simpler habit.
**Single quotes** stop all expansion, as in @sec-shell-basics: `'$d'` is
the two characters `$d`. Use double quotes when you want the value,
single quotes when you want the text exactly as typed.

**A misspelled variable is empty, not an error.** Set a variable and
then use it with a typo, through `echo` so nothing happens:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
outdir=~/bioinf-computing-ch08/out
echo "would delete: $outdri/"
```

```{.console}
would delete: /
```

`outdri` was never set, so bash replaced it with nothing, silently.
Inside a real command such as `rm -rf "$outdri/"`, the quotes would
faithfully hand `rm` the one argument `/`: the wrong path, built by a
typo. What `rm` then does depends on its safeguards and your
permissions; the point is that the command was built wrong and nothing
warned you. Never run that line. @sec-shell-scripts-strict shows the
setting, `set -u`, that turns an unset variable into an error.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: a misspelled variable is empty
`rm -rf "$outdri/"` with `outdri` unset is handed the argument `/`.
Quotes keep an argument whole, but they do not check that it is the path
you meant. Preview any command built from variables by putting `echo` in
front of it, and use `set -u` in scripts (@sec-shell-scripts-strict).
:::

Two naming habits avoid trouble. Use **lower-case names** for your own
variables (`d`, `outdir`, `sample`): upper-case names such as `PATH`,
`HOME`, and `USER` belong to the system (@sec-linux-system-variables),
and overwriting `PATH` inside a script stops it finding any command.
And use names that say what the value is: `fastq` tells the next reader
more than `x`.

### The expansions you have already met

Several pieces of syntax from earlier chapters are expansions too, and
the quoting rule applies to all of them.

**Command substitution, `$( )`**, runs a command and puts its output in
its place. @sec-organizing-projects's script names its log with
`$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M%S)`, and @sec-linux-system stored a field with
`f=$(…)`. Quote it like a variable: `"$(date +%Y-%m-%d)"`.

**Arithmetic, `$(( ))`**, does whole-number arithmetic. Now
@sec-orientation's read count can be taken apart. Run the inner part
first, then the whole line:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | wc -l
echo $(( $(gunzip -c ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))
```

```{.console}
200000
50000
```

The inner `$( )` runs the pipeline and becomes `200000`, the number of
lines; `$(( 200000 / 4 ))` becomes `50000`, one read per four lines.
Bash arithmetic is integers only: `$(( 7 / 2 ))` is `3`. Anything with
decimals belongs in R or Python (@sec-r-essentials,
@sec-python-essentials) or `awk` (@sec-text-tools).

**Braces, `${name}`**, mark where a variable's name ends. Compare:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
sample=WT_REP1
echo "$sample_R1.fastq.gz"
echo "${sample}_R1.fastq.gz"
```

```{.console}
.fastq.gz
WT_REP1_R1.fastq.gz
```

In the first line, bash read the longest name it could, `sample_R1`,
which is unset and so empty. Braces end the name where you mean it to:
use `"${sample}_R1.fastq.gz"` whenever a name is followed by a letter,
digit, or `_`.

**Trimming a value.** Inside braces, `#`, `%`, and `/` cut or replace
part of a value without starting another program. On a path from the
practice folder:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
f="Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz"
echo "${f##*/}"
echo "${f%.gz}"
echo "${f/_R1/_R2}"
basename "$f"
```

```{.console}
sample_C_R1.fq.gz
Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq
Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz
sample_C_R1.fq.gz
```

`${f##*/}` removes everything up to the last `/`, which leaves the file
name, the same as the `basename` command. `${f%.gz}` removes `.gz` from
the end. `${f/_R1/_R2}` replaces the first `_R1` with `_R2`, which
@sec-shell-scripts-loops uses to find the partner of each R1 file.
@tbl-expansions collects these forms.

: Expansions, with examples on `f="Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz"` and the `rows` list below. Quote every one of them. {#tbl-expansions}

| Form | Gives | Example | Output |
|:-----|:------|:--------|:-------|
| `"$f"` | the value, as one word | `echo "$f"` | `Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz` |
| `"${f}"` | the same; braces mark where the name ends | `"${sample}_R1.fastq.gz"` | `WT_REP1_R1.fastq.gz` |
| `"$(cmd)"` | the output of a command | `"$(date +%Y-%m-%d)"` | today's date |
| `$(( expr ))` | whole-number arithmetic | `$(( 200000 / 4 ))` | `50000` |
| `"${f##*/}"` | remove up to the last `/` | `"${f##*/}"` | `sample_C_R1.fq.gz` |
| `"${f%.gz}"` | remove an ending | `"${f%.gz}"` | `Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq` |
| `"${f/_R1/_R2}"` | replace the first match | `"${f/_R1/_R2}"` | `Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz` |
| `"${rows[@]}"` | every item of a list, each as its own word | `printf '[%s] ' "${rows[@]}"` | `[sample] [run_folder] …` |
| `${#rows[@]}` | the number of items in a list | `echo "${#rows[@]}"` | `28` |

### Lists

@sec-shell-basics and @sec-text-tools built the sample table from a
list, `rows=(…)`, and promised an explanation. A **list** (bash calls it
an array) holds several values under one name. Paste the same list
again:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
rows=(sample run_folder condition reads
  sample_C "Run 3 final" treated 12
  sample_A run1 control 9
  sample_B run2 control 30
  sample_E run5 treated 105
  sample_B run2 control 30
  sample_D run4 control 8)
echo "${#rows[@]} items"
echo "${rows[5]}"
```

```{.console}
28 items
Run 3 final
```

The quotes around `"Run 3 final"` in the list made it one item, so the
list has 28 items, not 30. Items are numbered from 0: `${rows[5]}` is
the sixth, `Run 3 final`. `"${rows[@]}"`, in double quotes, gives every
item as its own word, spaces kept. The table itself came from one
`printf`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "${rows[@]}"
```

`printf` takes a format and fills each `%s` with the next item. When it
has more items than `%s` slots, it **reuses the format** until the items
run out: four slots, 28 items, so seven lines of four tab-separated
columns. A small case shows the rule:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
printf '%s-%s\n' a b c d e
```

```{.console}
a-b
c-d
e-
```

Prefer `printf` to `echo` for anything with tabs, backslashes, or a
format: `printf` treats `\t` and `\n` the same way everywhere, while
`echo`'s handling of them differs between shells and systems. `echo` is
fine for a plain message.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** (a) `sample=WT_REP1; echo "$sample_R1.fastq.gz"`.
What prints? (b) `f="Run 3 final/a.fq.gz"; ls $f`: how many names does
`ls` receive?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
(a) `.fastq.gz`. Bash read a variable called `sample_R1`, which is
unset, so it became nothing. Write `"${sample}_R1.fastq.gz"`. (b) Three:
`Run`, `3`, and `final/a.fq.gz`, because the unquoted value is split at
its spaces. `ls "$f"` receives one.
:::
:::

## Loops {#sec-shell-scripts-loops}

Count the reads in every R1 file of the practice folder. Here is the
version most people write first. It has two bugs; run it and look for
them in the output:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
for f in */*_R1*; do n=$(gunzip -c $f | wc -l); echo "$f $((n/4))"; done
```

```{.console}
gzip: Run.gz: No such file or directory
gzip: 3.gz: No such file or directory
gzip: final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz: No such file or directory
Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz 0
run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz 2
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz 3
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp 3
```

The exit status is 0. Sample C really has 4 reads, and the last line is
the stray temporary copy from @sec-shell-basics, counted as if it were
a sample. Neither bug stopped the loop or changed its exit status; the
three error lines are the only hint, and in a long run they scroll past.
(GNU `gunzip` tries adding `.gz` to a name it cannot find, which is why
it reports `Run.gz`; a Mac's `gunzip` prints `gunzip: can't stat: Run`
and so on.)

Fix one bug at a time. First quote `"$f"`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
for f in */*_R1*; do n=$(gunzip -c "$f" | wc -l); echo "$f $((n/4))"; done
```

```{.console}
Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz 4
run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz 2
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz 3
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp 3
```

Sample C now arrives as one name and gives 4. Then tighten the pattern
so it only matches names that end the way FASTQ files end, `.fastq.gz`
or `.fq.gz`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz; do n=$(gunzip -c "$f" | wc -l); echo "$f $((n/4))"; done
```

```{.console}
Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz 4
run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz 2
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz 3
```

Three samples, three correct counts. (The lines may come out in a
different order on your system: the order of a wildcard's matches
depends on the language settings. On these machines `Run 3 final`
sorted first; on several Linux clusters it sorts last. The counts are
what matter.)

**What a `for` loop does.** The general form is:

```{.bash filename="the form of a for loop"}
for name in list; do
  commands that use "$name"
done
```

Bash expands the list **once**, before the loop starts: here the
wildcard became the list of matching file names. Then it runs the
commands once per item, with `f` set to each in turn. The one-line
version above just puts `;` where the line breaks would be. In a
script, write it on several lines and indent the body, as in the box.

Loop over a wildcard, never over the output of `ls`: `for f in $(ls)`
splits the names at their spaces, exactly like an unquoted variable.

**Preview first.** A loop repeats a command many times, so a mistake is
repeated too. Before a loop that changes files, put `echo` in front of
the command and read what it would do:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz; do echo cp "$f" ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/; done
```

```{.console}
cp Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch08/
cp run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch08/
cp run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch08/
```

This is @sec-shell-basics's habit with `rm`, now for loops. The list is
right, so the real loop would copy three files. (`echo` joins its
arguments with spaces, so it cannot show that `Run 3 final/…` is one
argument; the quotes in the loop make sure it is.) When the list looks
right, remove `echo` and run it.

### When nothing matches

Try a pattern that matches nothing in the practice folder:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
for f in */*.bam; do echo "got: $f"; done
```

```{.console}
got: */*.bam
```

When a wildcard matches nothing, bash passes the pattern unchanged
(@sec-shell-basics-wildcards), so the loop ran once with `f` set to the
literal text `*/*.bam`. The next command would fail with a confusing
`No such file or directory` for a file called `*/*.bam`. Bash can be
told to drop a pattern that matches nothing instead:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
shopt -s nullglob
for f in */*.bam; do echo "got: $f"; done
shopt -u nullglob
```

With `nullglob` set the loop runs zero times and prints nothing;
`shopt -u` unsets it again in your terminal. In a script that loops over
a wildcard, put `shopt -s nullglob` near the top. But zero passes is not
a success either: a script that "processes" no files and exits 0 looks
exactly like one that worked. So store the matches in a list and stop
if it is empty:

```{.bash filename="in a script"}
shopt -s nullglob
files=(*/*_R1.f*q.gz)
if (( ${#files[@]} == 0 )); then echo "no R1 files found" >&2; exit 1; fi
for f in "${files[@]}"; do
  echo "would count $f"
done
```

These are script lines: typed into a terminal, the `exit` would close
it. `if` is explained in @sec-shell-scripts-conditionals and `>&2` in
@sec-shell-scripts-arguments; here they read "if the list has zero
items, print a message and stop".

**Numbered ranges.** Brace ranges from @sec-shell-basics work as a loop
list: `for i in {01..03}; do echo "sample_$i"; done` prints `sample_01`,
`sample_02`, `sample_03`.

### Paired files

Paired-end reads come as R1 and R2 files with matching names. From each
R1 name, build the R2 name with the replacement from
@tbl-expansions and check that the file exists (`-e`, "exists", is one
of the tests in @sec-shell-scripts-conditionals):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
for r1 in */*_R1.f*q.gz; do
  r2="${r1/_R1/_R2}"
  if [[ -e "$r2" ]]; then echo "pair: $r1 + $r2"; else echo "no R2 for $r1"; fi
done
```

```{.console}
pair: Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz + Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz
pair: run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz + run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
pair: run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz + run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
```

`${r1/_R1/_R2}` replaces the **first** `_R1` in the whole path. A
folder called `run_R1_old/` would break it, which is one more reason
for @sec-organizing-projects's naming rules: `_R1` and `_R2` appear only
once, just before the file ending.

### Rows of a table

A sample table and the files on disk can disagree, as @sec-text-tools
warned. Check each row of the practice table against the folders:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
tail -n +2 meta/samples.tsv | while IFS=$'\t' read -r sample folder cond reads; do # <1>
  if [[ -d "$folder" ]]; then echo "$sample: folder '$folder' found"
  else echo "$sample: folder '$folder' MISSING"; fi
done
```
1. `tail -n +2` skips the header line; `read` takes one line at a time
   from the pipe.

```{.console}
sample_C: folder 'Run 3 final' found
sample_A: folder 'run1' found
sample_B: folder 'run2' found
sample_E: folder 'run5' MISSING
sample_B: folder 'run2' found
sample_D: folder 'run4' MISSING
```

Two rows point at folders that do not exist. Three details make this
loop work:

- `while … read …; do … done` runs once per **line** of its input, and
  stops when there are no more lines.
- `IFS=$'\t'` sets, for this `read` only, the characters it splits a
  line at: tabs only. So `Run 3 final` arrives whole in `folder`,
  spaces and all. (`$'\t'` is bash's way to write a tab character.)
- `read -r` keeps backslashes as they are, instead of treating them as
  escapes. Always use `-r`.

`read` puts the first field in `sample`, the second in `folder`, and so
on; the last name gets whatever is left.

The tempting alternative loops over the table's words:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
for line in $(tail -n +2 meta/samples.tsv | head -n 2); do printf '[%s] ' "$line"; done; echo
```

```{.console}
[sample_C] [Run] [3] [final] [treated] [12] [sample_A] [run1] [control] [9]
```

`$( )` unquoted is split at spaces, tabs, and newlines alike, so the
"lines" arrive one word at a time, and `Run 3 final` falls apart.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: loop over files with a wildcard, over lines with `while read`
`for f in $(ls)` and `for line in $(cat file)` split at every space.
Loop over files with a wildcard (`for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz`), and over
the lines of a table with `while IFS=$'\t' read -r …; do … done`.
:::

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "`for line in $(cat file)` goes through a file line by line"
**Reality.** It goes word by word, split at spaces and tabs, and it
matches wildcards. Read lines with `while IFS= read -r line`.
:::

**A loop at the end of a pipe forgets.** Bash runs each part of a pipe
in its own process (a **subshell**), including a `while` loop at the
end. Variables set inside the loop disappear with that process. It
matters as soon as a loop must remember something, such as "did any row
fail?":

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
bad=0
tail -n +2 meta/samples.tsv | while IFS=$'\t' read -r sample folder _; do
  if [[ ! -d "$folder" ]]; then bad=1; fi
done
echo "bad after the loop: $bad"
```

```{.console}
bad after the loop: 0
```

Two folders are missing, yet `bad` is still 0: the `bad=1` happened in
the subshell. A script that ended with `exit "$bad"` would report
success. (`_` is the usual name for "a value I don't need"; here it
takes the rest of the line.) The repair feeds the file to the loop
with `<` instead of a pipe, so the loop runs in the script's own shell.
You will use it, ready-made, in exercise 2:

```{.bash filename="in a script"}
bad=0
{
  IFS= read -r _   # skip the header line
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r sample folder rest || [[ -n "$sample$folder$rest" ]]; do
    if [[ ! -d "$folder" ]]; then
      printf '%s: missing folder %s\n' "$sample" "$folder" >&2
      bad=1
    fi
  done
} < "$table"
exit "$bad"
```

The `< "$table"` after the closing `}` feeds the file to everything
inside the braces. The first `read` takes the header line; the `while`
loop gets the rest. Because nothing here is a pipe, `bad=1` survives
the loop and the script can exit with it. The extra `|| [[ -n
"$sample$folder$rest" ]]` handles a last line with no newline at its
end: `read` still fills the variables but reports failure, so a plain
`while read` would skip that row without a word. The test says "or
the line was not empty", so the last row is checked too. (When you only need a total,
`awk` from @sec-text-tools is simpler than a loop.)

**Limits of `read`.** This way of reading a table is for simple,
tidy tables like the practice one, where every field is filled in. A
tab counts as "white space" to `read`, so two tabs in a row do not
give an empty field. A row with an empty folder field,
`sample_C<TAB><TAB>control<TAB>12`, gives `folder=control`, `cond=12`,
and an empty `reads`, silently shifted. And a plain `while read` loop
skips a last line that has no newline after it (the repair above
deals with that one). Real sample sheets are read with R or Python
(@sec-tabular-data).

**Windows line endings, inside a loop.** @sec-linux-system-line-endings
showed that a file saved by Excel ends each line in a carriage return,
`\r`. Read the practice CSV with `IFS=,` and look at the last field:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
tail -n +2 meta/samples_from_excel.csv | head -n 1 | while IFS=, read -r sample folder cond reads; do
  if [[ "$reads" == 12 ]]; then echo "reads is 12"; else echo "reads is not 12"; fi
  (( reads > 10 )) && echo big
done
```

```{.console}
reads is not 12
bash: ((: 12: arithmetic syntax error: invalid arithmetic operator (error token is "")
```

The value is really `12\r`, so it is never equal to `12`, and arithmetic
on it fails. (The exact wording of the error differs between bash
versions.) The `\r` sits in the **last** field: a loop that only used
the folder name would never notice it. `IFS=,` also works only for a
simple file like this one, with no commas inside quoted fields; it is
not a CSV reader. Look at any table with `cat -A` before a script
relies on it, and fix the line endings first
(@sec-linux-system-line-endings). @tbl-loop-patterns sums up the
section.

: Loop patterns. {#tbl-loop-patterns}

| Task | Pattern | Pitfall it avoids |
|:-----|:--------|:------------------|
| Every file matching a pattern | `for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz; do … "$f" …; done` | names with spaces split; stray files matched by a loose pattern |
| Pattern may match nothing | `shopt -s nullglob`, a list, and a check that it is not empty | a loop over the literal pattern; a "success" on no files |
| R1/R2 pairs | `r2="${r1/_R1/_R2}"`, then `[[ -e "$r2" ]]` | a missing partner noticed only later |
| A numbered range | `for i in {01..03}; do …; done` | typing the list by hand |
| Rows of a TSV | `while IFS=$'\t' read -r a b c; do …; done` | fields split at spaces |
| Rows, remembering something | `{ …; while read …; done; } < "$table"` | a variable lost in a pipe's subshell |
| Don't: | `for f in $(ls)` | names split at spaces |
| Don't: | `for line in $(cat file)` | lines split into words |

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** A loop `for f in data/raw/*.fq.gz; do seqkit stats
"$f"; done` prints an error for a file called `data/raw/*.fq.gz`, then
stops. The folder holds `SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz` and
`SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz`. Why, and what would `shopt -s nullglob` have
changed?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
No file matched, so bash passed the pattern unchanged and the loop ran
once with `f` set to `data/raw/*.fq.gz`. The files end in `.fastq.gz`,
not `.fq.gz`. With `nullglob` the loop would have run zero times, so a
script should also check that its list is not empty.
:::
:::

## Exit status and conditionals {#sec-shell-scripts-conditionals}

Every command finishes with an **exit status**, a number you saw with
`echo $?` in @sec-getting-help: 0 means success, anything else a kind
of failure. `grep` uses three (@sec-text-tools): 0 found a match, 1
found none, 2 something went wrong. Check them in the practice folder:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
grep -q sample_E meta/samples.tsv; echo "status $?"
grep -q sample_F meta/samples.tsv; echo "status $?"
grep -q sample_E nope.tsv; echo "status $?"
```

```{.console}
status 0
status 1
grep: nope.tsv: No such file or directory
status 2
```

(`-q`, quiet, makes `grep` print nothing; only its status matters.)
@sec-linux-system used one such status to choose what to print. Run it
for a sample that is listed and one that is not:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
grep -q sample_E meta/samples.tsv && echo listed || echo "not listed"
grep -q sample_F meta/samples.tsv && echo listed || echo "not listed"
```

```{.console}
listed
not listed
```

`&&` runs the next command only if the one before it succeeded (status
0); `||` runs the next only if it failed. `a && b || c` looks like
"if a then b else c", but it is not quite: `c` also runs when `b`
fails. `true && false || echo "c ran anyway"` prints `c ran anyway`. For
anything more than a one-liner, use `if`.

**`if` tests a command's exit status, and nothing else.** The form is:

```{.bash filename="the form of if"}
if command; then
  commands to run when it succeeds
elif other_command; then
  commands when the first failed and this one succeeds
else
  commands when all of them failed
fi
```

`elif` and `else` are optional. Any command can follow `if`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
if grep -q sample_D meta/samples.tsv; then echo "sample_D is in the table"; else echo "no sample_D"; fi
```

```{.console}
sample_D is in the table
```

**Tests with `[[ … ]]`.** Most `if`s ask a question about a file, a
string, or a number. `[[ … ]]` is a command that does nothing except
answer such a question with its exit status:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
f="Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz"
if [[ -f "$f" ]]; then echo "file exists"; fi
if [[ -s "$f" ]]; then echo "and is not empty"; fi
if [[ -d run5 ]]; then echo "run5 found"; else echo "no folder run5"; fi
x=""
if [[ -z "$x" ]]; then echo "x is empty"; fi
```

```{.console}
file exists
and is not empty
no folder run5
x is empty
```

The spaces inside `[[ ` and ` ]]` are required: `[[-f "$f"]]` is an
error. @tbl-tests lists the tests you will use most.

: Tests for `[[ … ]]` and `(( … ))`. {#tbl-tests}

| Test | True when | Example |
|:-----|:----------|:--------|
| `-e path` | it exists (file, folder, or other) | `[[ -e "$r2" ]]` |
| `-f path` | it is a regular file | `[[ -f "$1" ]]` |
| `-d path` | it is a folder | `[[ -d "$folder" ]]` |
| `-s path` | it exists and is not empty | `[[ -s results/counts.tsv ]]` |
| `-r path` | you may read it | `[[ -r "$table" ]]` |
| `a == b`, `a != b` | the strings are the same, or differ | `[[ "$ext" == gz ]]` |
| `-z s`, `-n s` | the string is empty, or not empty | `[[ -z "$x" ]]` |
| `a -eq b`, `-ne`, `-lt`, `-le`, `-gt`, `-ge` | numbers: equal, not equal, less than, … | `[[ "$n" -gt 0 ]]` |
| `(( a < b ))`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `==`, `!=` | numbers, written as arithmetic | `(( n > 0 ))` |
| **Trap:** `[[ 9 < 30 ]]` | false: `<` inside `[[ ]]` compares **text** | use `(( 9 < 30 ))` or `-lt` |
| `! test` | the test is false | `[[ ! -d "$folder" ]]` |

**The trap in the table.** Inside `[[ ]]`, `<` and `>` compare text, in
dictionary order, not numbers:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
[[ 9 < 30 ]]; echo "status $?"
(( 9 < 30 )); echo "status $?"
[[ 9 -lt 30 ]]; echo "status $?"
```

```{.console}
status 1
status 0
status 0
```

As text, `9` comes after `3`, so `[[ 9 < 30 ]]` is false, the same
mistake as `sort` without `-n` in @sec-text-tools. For numbers, use
`(( ))` or the letter tests (`-lt`, `-gt`, …).

You will also meet the older single-bracket test, `[ … ]` (for example
`[ 9 -lt 30 ]`, also true). It works in every shell, not only bash, but
every variable inside it must be quoted, and it lacks some features.
This book uses `[[ ]]` in bash scripts.

**`case`, for matching patterns.** When one value can match several
patterns, `case` is tidier than a chain of `elif`s. You will see it in
other people's scripts; recognising it is enough here:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
f="Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz"
case "$f" in
  *.fq.gz|*.fastq.gz) echo "FASTQ: $f" ;;
  *)                  echo "skip: $f" ;;
esac
```

```{.console}
FASTQ: Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
```

Each pattern ends in `)`, `|` means "or", `;;` ends a branch, and `*)`
catches everything else.

**A script's own exit status.** A script exits with the status of the
last command it ran, unless it calls `exit` first. `exit 0` reports
success; any other number, usually `exit 1`, reports failure. The next
program, or you with `echo $?`, can then tell whether it worked.
Scripts that stop early on a problem use exactly this, as the next
section shows.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** `n=9; if [[ $n < 10 ]]; then echo small; else echo
big; fi`. What prints, and how do you fix it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`big`. Inside `[[ ]]`, `<` compares text, and `9` sorts after `1`.
`if (( n < 10 ))` or `if [[ "$n" -lt 10 ]]` prints `small`. The
unquoted `$n` is not the problem: `[[ ]]` does not split its contents
(@sec-shell-scripts-variables).
:::
:::

## Script arguments {#sec-shell-scripts-arguments}

`gtf_types.sh` always reads the same file. A useful script works on the
files you give it. @sec-linux-system's exercise 1 left you a script that
does: `count_lines.sh`. Run it again on the practice table (if you
skipped that exercise, the script is the one-line file below; save it as
`~/bioinf-computing-ch07/bin/count_lines.sh` and `chmod u+x` it):

```{.bash filename="~/bioinf-computing-ch07/bin/count_lines.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count_lines.sh: print a file name and its number of lines
printf "%s: %s lines\n" "$(basename "$1")" "$(wc -l < "$1")"
```

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
~/bioinf-computing-ch07/bin/count_lines.sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/meta/samples.tsv
```

```{.console}
samples.tsv: 7 lines
```

Now every piece can be read. `$1` is the **first argument**, the first
word after the script's name: here the path to `samples.tsv`. `"$(wc -l
< "$1")"` runs `wc -l` on that file and puts its count in place.
`"$(basename "$1")"` puts the file name without its folders. `printf`
fills its two `%s` with the two values. The quotes inside the `$( )`
are separate from the ones outside, so both sets are needed.

**What a script receives.** Save this script in your scratch folder. It
prints what it was given, in two ways:

```{.bash filename="~/bioinf-computing-ch08/args.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# args.sh: show what a script receives as arguments.
if [[ $# -lt 1 ]]; then # <1>
  echo "usage: args.sh ARG [ARG ...]" >&2 # <2>
  exit 2
fi
echo "script name (\$0): $0"
echo "number of arguments (\$#): $#"
echo 'with "$@":'
for a in "$@"; do echo "  [$a]"; done
echo 'with $* (unquoted):'
for a in $*; do echo "  [$a]"; done # <3>
```
1. `$#` is the number of arguments. Fewer than one: print how to use
   the script and stop.
2. `>&2` sends the message to stderr (below).
3. Deliberately wrong, for comparison; ShellCheck flags it
   (@sec-shell-scripts-debugging).

Run it with two arguments, one with spaces in it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08
chmod u+x args.sh
./args.sh a.fq.gz "Run 3 final/c.fq.gz"
```

```{.console}
script name ($0): ./args.sh
number of arguments ($#): 2
with "$@":
  [a.fq.gz]
  [Run 3 final/c.fq.gz]
with $* (unquoted):
  [a.fq.gz]
  [Run]
  [3]
  [final/c.fq.gz]
```

The script received two arguments, and `"$@"` gives exactly those two,
each kept whole. Unquoted `$*` joins them and splits the result at
spaces, giving four. **Always pass a script's arguments on as
`"$@"`, in quotes**: `for f in "$@"` loops over the files the user
gave, however they are named. @tbl-special-params lists these names
and the others you will meet.

: Special parameters, with `./args.sh a.fq.gz "Run 3 final/c.fq.gz"`. {#tbl-special-params}

| Name | Holds | Example value |
|:-----|:------|:--------------|
| `$0` | the name the script was started as | `./args.sh` |
| `$1`, `$2`, … `$9` | the first, second, … ninth argument | `$2` is `Run 3 final/c.fq.gz` |
| `${10}` | the tenth argument (braces needed from 10 on) | (empty here) |
| `$#` | the number of arguments | `2` |
| `"$@"` | every argument, each as its own word | `a.fq.gz`, `Run 3 final/c.fq.gz` |
| `$*` | every argument joined into one string; unquoted, split again | four words |
| `$?` | the exit status of the last command | `0` after a success |
| `$$` | the process number of this shell or script | a number such as `48213` |

**A usage check.** Run `args.sh` with no arguments, and then with its
output sent to a file:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
./args.sh; echo "exit $?"
./args.sh > out.txt; echo "exit $?"
cat out.txt
```

```{.console}
usage: args.sh ARG [ARG ...]
exit 2
usage: args.sh ARG [ARG ...]
exit 2
```

The check at the top caught the mistake before the script did any
work, said how to use it, and exited with a nonzero status. Two
details make it a good check:

- **`>&2` sends the message to stderr**, the error stream from
  @sec-text-tools-streams. So even with `> out.txt` the message still
  appears on the screen, and `out.txt` stays empty: a results file
  never ends up holding an error message. Every message from a script
  (warnings, progress, usage) goes to stderr; only results go to
  stdout.
- **Exit status 2** is the usual convention for "used wrongly", and 1
  for "tried, and something failed". Any nonzero status tells the
  caller to stop.

Every script that takes arguments should start with a check like this.
A script that needs exactly one file checks `if [[ $# -ne 1 ]]`.

**Options.** Many tools take options such as `--threads 4` or `-o
out.tsv`. Bash can parse them (with a built-in called `getopts`), but
it takes more code than it saves at this stage; @sec-reusable-code
returns to it. When a script's arguments get complicated, that is a
sign it may be better written in R or Python (@sec-r-essentials,
@sec-python-essentials).

**Arguments, a variable at the top, or a settings file?** A script can
get its inputs in three ways (@tbl-script-inputs). This book uses
arguments for the files a script works on, and a variable near the top
for settings that rarely change.

: Three ways to give a script its inputs. {#tbl-script-inputs}

| Way | Example | Use it for |
|:----|:--------|:-----------|
| Arguments | `./count_reads.sh run1/*.fastq.gz` | the files to work on: they change each run |
| A variable at the top | `threads=4` on line 10 | settings that rarely change; easy to find and edit |
| A settings file | `source config.sh` | many settings shared by several scripts; later, workflow managers' parameter files (@sec-workflow-managers) |

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** You run `./run.sh "sample A.fq.gz" b.fq.gz`. What
are `$#` and `$1`? And why does the script print its usage message with
`>&2`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`$#` is `2` and `$1` is `sample A.fq.gz`: the quotes on the command line
made it one argument. `>&2` sends the message to stderr, so with `>
results.tsv` it still appears on the screen and the results file holds
only results.
:::
:::

**End of sitting A.** You can now save commands as a script, quote
values, loop over files and table rows, test conditions, and take file
names as arguments. That is enough for **exercise 1, part A**
(@sec-shell-scripts-exercises): fixing a supplied `count_reads.sh` that
gets sample C wrong and counts the stray `.tmp` file. Part B, and
everything else in the second half, is about making scripts
dependable: what happens when a command inside them fails.

The first sitting was about **writing** scripts: saving commands,
quoting, loops, tests, and arguments. The second is about **making them
dependable**: stopping when something fails, keeping results and
messages apart, reading a real script line by line, chaining steps into
a small pipeline, finding bugs, and saving each working version with
git. If you are starting a new sitting, go back to your scratch folder
first:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08
```

## Stopping on errors: `set -euo pipefail` {#sec-shell-scripts-strict}

In @sec-orientation, a pitfall said that the shell does not stop on
errors unless told to. Here is what that means inside a script. Make a
five-line script, `count.sh`: open it with `code count.sh` (or `nano
count.sh`), paste, and save.

```{.bash filename="count.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count.sh: count the reads in one gzipped FASTQ file.
n=$(gunzip -c "$1" | wc -l)
echo "$1: $(( n / 4 )) reads"
echo "done"
```

Copy one practice file next to it (a copy, so the practice folder stays
as it is), make the script executable, and run it three ways: on the
copy, on a file that does not exist, and with no argument at all.

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cp ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz .
chmod u+x count.sh
./count.sh sample_A_R1.fastq.gz; echo "exit $?"
./count.sh missing.fastq.gz; echo "exit $?"
./count.sh; echo "exit $?"
```

```{.console}
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz: 2 reads
done
exit 0
gzip: missing.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
missing.fastq.gz: 0 reads
done
exit 0
gunzip: can't stat:  (.gz): No such file or directory
: 0 reads
done
exit 0
```

(The error lines come from gzip, and their wording varies: GNU gzip on
Linux says `gzip: missing.fastq.gz: No such file or directory`; Apple's
on a Mac says `gunzip: can't stat: …`. The last block is from a Mac.)

The first run is right. The other two are wrong in a quiet way. `gunzip`
failed and said so, but bash went on to the next line, `wc -l` counted
the zero lines it was given, and the script printed `0 reads`, then
`done`, and finished with exit status 0, which means success. A script
that ran later steps on this "result" would never know.

Now add **one line** after the comment, so that the script reads:

```{.bash filename="count.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count.sh: count the reads in one gzipped FASTQ file.
set -euo pipefail
n=$(gunzip -c "$1" | wc -l)
echo "$1: $(( n / 4 )) reads"
echo "done"
```

Run the same three commands again:

```{.console}
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz: 2 reads
done
exit 0
gzip: missing.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
exit 1
./count.sh: line 4: $1: unbound variable
exit 1
```

The good run is unchanged. The missing file now stops the script at the
failed line, with no count and exit status 1. The missing argument stops
it before `gunzip` even starts, with a message that names the line and
the problem (@fig-strict-mode).

::: {#fig-strict-mode}
{{< svg ../figures/strict-mode.svg >}}

The same script run on a missing file, without and with `set -euo
pipefail`. Without it, bash goes on past the error and reports a wrong
count with exit status 0; with it, the script stops at the failure with
exit status 1 and no result. The strips below show what strict mode
gets wrong: it stops on a `grep` that simply found nothing, and on
`head` closing a pipe, and it cannot see a tool that reports success on
bad input.
:::

**Now name each letter.** `set` changes how bash behaves for the rest
of the script. The three settings are independent, and each has its
own demonstration (all are small scripts you can make the same way as
`count.sh`).

- **`-e`: stop when a command fails.** A command "fails" when its exit
  status is not 0 (@sec-getting-help). By default bash just moves on to
  the next line, which is @sec-orientation's pitfall.
- **`-u`: an unset variable is an error, not an empty value.** This is
  @sec-shell-scripts-variables's misspelled `$outdri`, which silently
  became empty and turned `"$outdri/"` into `/`. With `set -u`:

  ```{.bash filename="typo.sh"}
  #!/usr/bin/env bash
  set -u
  outdir=~/bioinf-computing-ch08/out
  echo "would delete: $outdri/"
  ```

  ```{.console}
  ./typo.sh: line 4: outdri: unbound variable
  ```

  The script stops (exit status 1) and names the misspelled variable.
- **`-o pipefail`: a pipeline fails if any command in it fails.**
  Without it, a pipeline's exit status is that of its **last**
  command. In `gunzip -c missing.gz | wc -l`, `gunzip` fails but `wc`
  succeeds, so the whole line "succeeds", and `-e` alone has nothing to
  stop on:

  ```{.bash filename="pipe.sh"}
  #!/usr/bin/env bash
  set -e
  lines=$(gunzip -c missing.gz | wc -l)
  echo "lines=$lines"
  echo "still running"
  ```

  ```{.console}
  gzip: missing.gz: No such file or directory
  lines=0
  still running
  ```

  Exit status 0. Change the second line to `set -eo pipefail` and the
  script stops after the gzip error, with exit status 1. This is the
  `pipefail` that @sec-text-tools promised. To see each command's status
  yourself, bash keeps them in a list, `PIPESTATUS`, right after a
  pipeline: `gunzip -c missing.gz | wc -l; echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}"`
  prints the count (`0`) and then `1 0`, one status per command.

**Then what it does not catch.** Strict mode is the book's rule for
every script, but it reacts only to exit statuses, and only in some
places. Five things to know, each captured from a real run:

**1. A "failure" that is not one.** `grep` exits with 1 when it finds
no match (@sec-text-tools). In a strict script, that stops everything,
silently:

```{.bash filename="grep1.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
n=$(grep -c ZZZ names.txt)
echo "n=$n"
```

With a `names.txt` that does not contain `ZZZ`, this prints nothing and
exits with 1. The tempting fix is `n=$(grep -c ZZZ names.txt || true)`:
"if it fails, succeed anyway". It does print `n=0`. But `grep` has a
second failure status, **2**, for a real error such as a missing or
unreadable file, and `|| true` swallows that too. With a misspelled
file name:

```{.console}
grep: missing.txt: No such file or directory
n=
```

Exit status 0, and `n` is empty. The script carries on with no number,
which is exactly what strict mode was meant to prevent. Keep the two
statuses apart instead:

```{.bash filename="grep2.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
file=names.txt
if n=$(grep -c ZZZ "$file"); then # <1>
  : # <2>
else
  status=$? # <3>
  [[ "$status" -eq 1 ]] || exit "$status" # <4>
fi
echo "n=$n"
```
1. A command inside an `if` does not trigger `-e`; the `if` looks at
   its status instead.
2. `:` is a command that does nothing and succeeds: here, "a match was
   found, carry on".
3. `$?` is `grep`'s status; save it before running anything else.
4. Status 1 (no match) is fine; anything else (2, an error) ends the
   script with that status.

With `names.txt` it prints `n=0` and exits 0. With `file=missing.txt` it
prints grep's error and exits with 2. When you only need a yes or no,
`if grep -q ZZZ "$file"; then …` is enough, but it treats a missing
file as "no", so check that the file is readable first (`[[ -r "$file"
]]`, @sec-shell-scripts-conditionals).

**2. `head` closing a pipe early.** In a strict script, try the
@sec-orientation idiom for a first look at a file, on the project's real
reads:

```{.bash filename="peek.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 1
echo "reached"
```

It prints the first header line and then stops, without `reached`,
with exit status **141**: in all six runs captured on Linux for this
book. `head` read its one line and exited; `gunzip`, still writing,
was stopped by the system (@sec-text-tools's `141`); and `pipefail`
reported that as a failure. `seq 1 1000000 | head -n 1` does the same.
On a tiny input, such as the practice folder's two-read file, the same
lines print `reached` and exit 0, because `gunzip` finished before
`head` exited. It is a matter of timing, not a guarantee either way,
so a script tested on toy data can fail on real data. Keep `| head`
for looking at files in the terminal, not inside strict scripts.
(`… | head -n 1 || true` would also hide a real decompression error,
so it is not the fix.)

**3. Commands that are being tested.** Commands tested by `if` and
`while` never trigger `-e`: their status is the test. That includes
everything inside a function called from an `if`:

```{.bash filename="func.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
f() { false; echo "after false in f"; }
if f; then echo ok; fi
```

```{.console}
after false in f
ok
```

In a chain with `&&` or `||`, only the commands **before the last**
are exempt. `false && echo skipped` does not stop a strict script (the
`false` is being tested); `true && false` does, with exit status 1
(the last `false` is not tested by anything).

**4. Masked statuses.** `local x=$(false)` inside a function, and
`export x=$(false)`, succeed: the status that `-e` sees is that of
`local` or `export`, which worked, not that of the command inside.
Declare and assign on separate lines (`local x`, then `x=$(…)`), and
the failure stops the script again.

**5. Tools that report success despite a problem.** This is
@sec-getting-help's finding, now inside a strict script. Give
@sec-organizing-projects's script a truncated read file, with a
checksum list made **after** the truncation (the mistake of making
checksums from a damaged copy):

```{.console}
checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: OK
command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz
[ERRO] data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: unexpected EOF
[ERRO]
output:   db1d8098fba21ca3be9934a6cc0dde37  results/read_counts.tsv
finished: 2026-11-22 15:45:39 -0600
```

seqkit 2.14.0 prints `[ERRO]` but exits 0, so strict mode sees nothing
wrong. The script finishes with exit status 0, and
`results/read_counts.tsv` holds **only the header line**. In the same
way, a gzip file that is valid but holds no reads gives `0 reads` and
passes both strict mode and `gzip -t`.

Strict mode only sees exit statuses. The remedy is to check what you
expect: a results file with more than a header line, a read count
above zero (or equal to the expected one), `gzip -t` before counting
(it catches a damaged stream, not a valid but empty one), and `md5sum
-c` against checksums made from the source (@sec-organizing-projects).
@sec-shell-scripts-read adds the first of these to @sec-organizing-projects's script.
@tbl-strict-mode sums up the section.

: What `set -euo pipefail` catches, and what it does not. {#tbl-strict-mode}

| Setting or case | Stops the script when | Does **not** catch | What to do |
|:----------------|:----------------------|:-------------------|:-----------|
| `-e` | a command exits nonzero | commands tested by `if`, `while`, or before the last `&&`/`\|\|` | nothing: by design |
| `-u` | an unset variable is used (`$outdri`) | a variable set to the wrong value | preview with `echo` |
| `-o pipefail` | any command in a pipeline fails | which command failed (see `PIPESTATUS`) | read the first error message |
| `grep` with no match | always (exit 1), although nothing is wrong | — | `if n=$(grep …)`; accept 1, exit on 2; never a blanket `\|\| true` |
| `… \| head` | often on real data (exit 141), rarely on toy data | — | keep `head` in the terminal |
| function called from `if` | — | failures inside the function | do not call work functions from `if` |
| `local x=$(cmd)` | — | `cmd` failing | `local x`, then `x=$(cmd)` |
| tool reports success on bad input | — | wrong or empty results | check outputs: counts, line numbers, `md5sum -c` |

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
`set -euo pipefail` stops a script when a command *reports* failure.
It cannot see a wrong result from a command that reports success, so
check the outputs too. Every script in this book starts with it: a
seatbelt, not a guarantee.
:::

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "With `set -euo pipefail` my script stops on every error"
**Reality.** It stops on a nonzero exit status, except in conditions,
functions called from conditions, all but the last command of an
`&&`/`||` chain, and masked assignments such as `local x=$(…)`. It
cannot see a tool that reports success on bad input, and it can stop
on harmless statuses (`grep` with no match, `head` closing a pipe).
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** Which of these stops a script that starts with `set
-euo pipefail`? (a) `grep -c XYZ file` with no match; (b) `seqkit stats`
(2.14.0) on a truncated file; (c) `gunzip -c missing.gz | wc -l`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
(a) Yes, with exit status 1, although nothing is wrong: put it in an
`if`, accept status 1, and keep status 2 (a real error) fatal, not a
blanket `|| true`. (b) No: seqkit prints `[ERRO]` but exits 0. (c) Yes,
thanks to `pipefail`; with `-e` alone it would not.
:::
:::

Exercise 1, part B and exercise 2 (@sec-shell-scripts-exercises) are
available from here.

## Logging output and errors {#sec-shell-scripts-logging}

Your finished `count_reads.sh` from exercise 1 prints one tab-separated
line per file. Run it with the two output streams of @sec-text-tools
sent to two different files: results (stdout) to `counts.tsv`, messages
(stderr) to `run.log`.

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh */*_R1.f*q.gz > ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/counts.tsv 2> ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/run.log
echo "exit $?"
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/counts.tsv
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/run.log
```

```{.console}
exit 0
sample_C_R1.fq.gz	4
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz	2
sample_B_R1.fastq.gz	3
```

The table is clean, and the log is empty. Now give it one good file and
one missing one, with the same redirections:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz missing.fastq.gz > ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/counts.tsv 2> ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/run.log
echo "exit $?"
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/counts.tsv
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/run.log
```

```{.console}
exit 1
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz	2
gzip: missing.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
```

The error went to the log, not into the table, and the script stopped
with exit status 1. Notice the table: it holds the line for the file
that worked. A table can look fine and still be incomplete; the exit
status and the log are what tell you the run failed.

**Now name it.** Results go to stdout; messages (progress, warnings,
errors, the usage line) go to stderr, in every script you write. Then
`> results.tsv` captures only results, and the messages still reach
your screen or a log.

A message to stderr is `echo "…" >&2`. For a script with several
messages, define two short **functions** once, near the top. A function
is a named group of commands (@sec-linux-system); this is the book's
first use of one:

```{.bash filename="part of a script"}
log() { printf '[%s] %s\n' "$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')" "$*" >&2; }
die() { log "ERROR: $*"; exit 1; }
```

`log "counting reads"` prints `[2026-11-22 14:26:50] counting reads` to
stderr; `die "missing input"` logs `ERROR: missing input` and ends the
script with status 1. Inside a function, `$*` is all its arguments
joined into one string: the one place this book joins arguments on
purpose. A function must be defined before the line that uses it.
Writing your own reusable functions is @sec-reusable-code.

**Keeping a log of a whole run.** @sec-organizing-projects's script
keeps everything it prints in a log file, with this form:

```{.bash filename="part of a script"}
log="$(mktemp "logs/01_count_reads_$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M%S)_XXXX.log")"
{
  …the commands…
} 2>&1 | tee "$log"
```

The `{ … }` group collects the output of all its commands; `2>&1` joins
stderr to stdout; `tee` shows that stream on the screen and writes it
to the log. The log name holds the date and time in the ISO form of
@sec-organizing-projects, and `mktemp` replaces `XXXX` with random
characters and creates the file, so two runs in the same second never
share a log. (This needs GNU `mktemp`, which fills in X's that come
before a suffix such as `.log`. The Mac's own `/usr/bin/mktemp` only
replaces X's at the very end, so without @sec-orientation's GNU tools
the log is literally named `…_XXXX.log` every run.)
@sec-shell-scripts-read takes this form apart line by line.

**Write to a temporary name, then `mv`.** @sec-text-tools showed that
`>` empties a file before the command starts, so a failed command can
leave a half-written result under the real name. Scripts in this book
write each output to `name.tmp` and move it into place only when the
step has succeeded:

```{.bash filename="part of a script"}
seqkit stats --quiet -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz > results/read_counts.tsv.tmp
mv results/read_counts.tsv.tmp results/read_counts.tsv
```

With `set -e`, a failure stops the script before `mv`, so a new result
is **published only after the step succeeds**, and a good result from
an earlier run is never replaced by a partial one. What this does not
do: after a failed rerun, the earlier run's finished file is still
there, and the half-written `.tmp` may be there too. So the rule is:
*publish a new result only after the step succeeds; on failure, an
older result may still exist, so use the run's exit status and log to
decide whether a result belongs to this run.*
@sec-shell-scripts-pipeline shows this on a real rerun. One assumption
is built in: a fixed `name.tmp` is fine while one run at a time writes
that output, as in this book's pipeline. Two runs at once would share
the `.tmp` (unique log names do not help with that), which needs unique
temporary names and more care than this chapter covers.

**What to log.** @sec-organizing-projects's list of what makes a result
traceable: start and end time, machine, tool versions, input checksums,
the exact command, and the output's checksum. To see every command as
bash runs it, there is `bash -x` (@sec-shell-scripts-debugging). @tbl-log-recipes collects the recipes.

: Recipes for output and logs. {#tbl-log-recipes}

| Goal | Recipe |
|:-----|:-------|
| Results to a file, messages to a log | `script.sh > results.tsv 2> run.log` |
| A message to stderr | `echo "…" >&2`, or a `log` function as above |
| Everything to the screen **and** a log | `{ …; } 2>&1 \| tee "$log"` **inside** a script that has `set -o pipefail`, as in `01` and `run_all.sh` |
| A dated log name that no other run shares | `mktemp "logs/name_$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M%S)_XXXX.log"` (GNU `mktemp`) |
| Publish a result only on success | write `name.tmp`, then `mv name.tmp name` (one run at a time) |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Tip
Write each output to `name.tmp`, then `mv` it into place, so a new
result is published only after the step succeeds. On failure an older
result may still exist: the exit status and the log say whether it
belongs to this run.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** Why does `count_reads.sh` print its usage message
with `>&2`? And after the run above with the missing file, what should
you trust: `counts.tsv`, or the exit status?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
So the message goes to stderr: with `> counts.tsv`, it stays on the
screen and the file holds only results. And the exit status (1): the
table looks fine but lacks the missing file's line.
:::
:::

## Reading Chapter 3's script, line by line {#sec-shell-scripts-read}

@sec-organizing-projects asked you to run `src/01_count_reads.sh` on
trust and promised that this chapter would explain every line. You now
know every piece. Look at it again:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cat ~/bioinf-computing/src/01_count_reads.sh
```

Before reading on, write in `NOTEBOOK.md`, in your own words, what each
line does. Use @fig-script-anatomy as the map of its parts. Then
compare with the annotations below (click a number to see its note).

```{.bash filename="src/01_count_reads.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash # <1>
# 01_count_reads.sh: check the raw FASTQ files, then count their reads. # <2>
# Run from the project folder:  pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh
set -euo pipefail # <3>

mkdir -p results logs # <4>
log="$(mktemp "logs/01_count_reads_$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M%S)_XXXX.log")" # <5>

{ # <6>
  echo "started:  $(date "+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z")" # <7>
  echo "host:     $(hostname)"
  echo "script:   $(md5sum src/01_count_reads.sh)" # <8>
  echo "seqkit:   $(seqkit version)" # <9>
  echo "checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:"
  (cd data/raw && md5sum -c checksums.md5) # <10>
  echo "command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz" # <11>
  seqkit stats --quiet -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz > results/read_counts.tsv.tmp # <12>
  mv results/read_counts.tsv.tmp results/read_counts.tsv # <13>
  echo "output:   $(md5sum results/read_counts.tsv)" # <14>
  echo "finished: $(date "+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z")" # <15>
} 2>&1 | tee "$log" # <16>
```
1. The shebang: run this file with the `bash` found on `PATH`
   (@sec-linux-system).
2. The header comment: what the script does, and how and from where to
   run it. Comments start with `#` and are ignored.
3. Strict mode (@sec-shell-scripts-strict): stop on any failure, any
   unset variable, any failing command in a pipeline.
4. Make the output folders; `-p` means no error if they already exist.
5. Nested substitutions, run inside out: `date` makes a time stamp,
   `mktemp` turns the name into a new, unique file, and `$( )` stores
   its name in `log` (@sec-shell-scripts-logging).
6. Start of a group: everything up to the closing `}` sends its output
   into one pipe (line 16).
7. `$( )` puts the current date and time into the line.
8. The script's own checksum: if anyone edits the script, this line in
   the log changes.
9. The tool's version, for the record.
10. A **subshell** in parentheses: the `cd` happens in a separate copy
    of the shell, so the next line still runs from the project folder.
    `&&` runs `md5sum -c` only if the `cd` worked. If a checksum fails,
    `md5sum` exits 1 and strict mode stops the script here.
11. The exact command, written to the log.
12. The real work, written to a temporary name.
13. Published under its real name only after the step succeeded.
14. The result's checksum, for the record.
15. A log with no `finished:` line means the run did not finish.
16. `2>&1` joins error messages to the normal output; `tee` shows both
    on the screen and writes them to the log.

**Then break it on purpose.** Never in `data/raw/`, which stays
read-only (@sec-organizing-projects). Copy the inputs, their checksums,
and the script to a scratch folder, make the copied reads writable,
and append one byte to one of them:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/proj-copy/data/raw ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/proj-copy/src
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/proj-copy
cp ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/*.fastq.gz ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/checksums.md5 data/raw/
cp ~/bioinf-computing/src/01_count_reads.sh src/
chmod u+w data/raw/*
printf 'x' >> data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
pixi run --manifest-path ~/bioinf-computing/pixi.toml bash src/01_count_reads.sh; echo "exit $?"
ls -A results
```

(`--manifest-path` tells pixi to use the project's environment while
you work in another folder.)

```{.console}
started:  2026-11-22 15:45:39 -0600
host:     your-laptop
script:   76fa8eb6a7b90f212042cfbe6d95cfcc  src/01_count_reads.sh
seqkit:   seqkit v2.14.0
checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: FAILED
md5sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match
exit 1
```

The script stopped at the checksum, exit status 1. `results/` is
empty: no `read_counts.tsv` and no `.tmp`. The log in `logs/` keeps the
failure. Why does it stop, when the failing command sits inside a group
whose output goes through a pipe to `tee`? The group runs in a
subshell that inherits `set -e`, so the subshell stops and exits 1;
`pipefail` then makes the whole pipeline fail despite `tee`'s success,
and `-e` stops the script. Remove `pipefail` (change line 4 to `set
-eu`) and rerun: the same `FAILED` lines print, but the script **exits
0**, because without `pipefail` the pipeline's status is `tee`'s.

**Run it from the wrong folder.** The script uses paths relative to
the project folder. Run it from your home folder instead:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~ && pixi run --manifest-path ~/bioinf-computing/pixi.toml bash bioinf-computing/src/01_count_reads.sh; echo "exit $?"
```

```{.console}
started:  2026-11-22 15:45:49 -0600
host:     your-laptop
md5sum: src/01_count_reads.sh: No such file or directory
script:
seqkit:   seqkit v2.14.0
checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:
bioinf-computing/src/01_count_reads.sh: line 15: cd: data/raw: No such file or directory
exit 1
```

It failed, but only at line 15, and it has already made empty
`results/` and `logs/` folders, plus a log file, in your home folder.
The `md5sum` failure on the `script:` line did not stop it either: a
command inside `echo "…$(…)"` is one more case `set -e` does not see.
Look with `ls ~/results ~/logs`; if they hold only this run's leftovers,
remove them (`rmdir ~/results` and `rm -r ~/logs`).

**Add a guard.** Open the real script, `code
~/bioinf-computing/src/01_count_reads.sh`, and add one line right after
`set -euo pipefail`:

```{.bash filename="src/01_count_reads.sh (new line 5)"}
[[ -f pixi.toml ]] || { echo "run from the project folder" >&2; exit 1; }
```

From `~`, the script now stops at once with `run from the project
folder` and exit status 1, and leaves nothing behind. The guard checks
for a file that only the project folder has, so it catches the common
mistake of running from the wrong folder; it does not prove that this
is the right project. (To repeat the broken-copy test above with the
guarded script, copy `~/bioinf-computing/pixi.toml` into `proj-copy/`
first, or it stops at the guard instead of the checksum.)

**Add a result check.** @sec-shell-scripts-strict showed this very
script finishing with exit status 0 and a `read_counts.tsv` holding
only its header line, because seqkit reported a damaged file but
exited 0. Strict mode cannot see that; a check of the result can. This
project always has two FASTQ files, so a good table has a header and
two rows. Add two lines right after the `seqkit stats` line, before
the `mv`:

```{.bash filename="src/01_count_reads.sh (after the seqkit line)"}
  [[ $(wc -l < results/read_counts.tsv.tmp) -eq 3 ]] ||
    { echo "read_counts: expected a header and 2 rows" >&2; exit 1; }
```

The number 3 belongs to this two-file project; a general script would
work out the expected number from its list of inputs. Rerun the
damaged-file case from @sec-shell-scripts-strict (a truncated R2 with
checksums made after the damage, in a copy) and the script now stops:

```{.console}
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: OK
command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz
[ERRO] data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: unexpected EOF
read_counts: expected a header and 2 rows
```

The exit status is 1, the `mv` never runs, and the previous good
`read_counts.tsv` stays as it was (the half-made `.tmp` is left
beside it). On the real files nothing changes: the same table, the
same output checksum. Your next run's log shows a new script checksum
(`f2857591…` instead of `76fa8eb6…`): that is exactly what the
`script:` line is for. You commit both changes in
@sec-shell-scripts-git.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
A failed step should stop the run, leave a log that says why, and
publish no new result.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** In the script, why is `(cd data/raw && md5sum -c
checksums.md5)` in parentheses?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
The parentheses make a subshell: the `cd` happens there and ends with
it, so the next line still runs from the project folder, where
`data/raw/*.fastq.gz` and `results/` are.
:::
:::

## Numbered scripts as a simple pipeline {#sec-shell-scripts-pipeline}

@sec-organizing-projects named scripts by their run order: `01_`,
`02_`, and so on. Now add the second step. It is
@sec-shell-scripts-first's `gtf_types.sh`, the GTF feature count from
@sec-text-tools, made into a project script. In `~/bioinf-computing`,
open `code src/02_gtf_summary.sh`, paste, and save:

```{.bash filename="src/02_gtf_summary.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# 02_gtf_summary.sh: count the feature types in the reference annotation.
# Run from the project folder:  pixi run bash src/02_gtf_summary.sh
# Input:  data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
# Output: results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv (feature, count; most common first)
set -euo pipefail

log() { printf '[%s] %s\n' "$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')" "$*" >&2; } # <1>
die() { log "ERROR: $*"; exit 1; }

[[ -f pixi.toml ]] || die "run from the project folder" # <2>

gtf="data/ref/genes.gtf.gz"
out="results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv"
[[ -s "$gtf" ]] || die "missing or empty: $gtf" # <3>

mkdir -p results
log "start; input md5: $(md5sum "$gtf")"
{
  printf 'feature\tcount\n' # <4>
  gunzip -c "$gtf" | cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr \
    | awk -v OFS='\t' '{print $2, $1}' # <5>
} > "$out.tmp"
mv "$out.tmp" "$out" # <6>
log "wrote $out ($(( $(wc -l < "$out") - 1 )) feature types)" # <7>
log "output md5: $(md5sum "$out")"
```
1. The `log` and `die` functions from @sec-shell-scripts-logging.
2. The guard from @sec-shell-scripts-read, using `die`.
3. Check the input exists and is not empty (`-s`) before starting.
4. A header line for the table.
5. @sec-text-tools's count, then `awk` swaps the two columns and
   separates them with a tab (`-v OFS='\t'`, also @sec-text-tools).
6. Published only after the step succeeded.
7. Lines in the file minus the header: the number of feature types.

`02` is deliberately shorter than `01`: its log lines go to the screen
(stderr), it keeps no log file of its own, and it records input and
output checksums but not tool versions (recording versions properly is
@sec-environments). The log file for the whole run comes from the next
script, `src/run_all.sh`, which runs every step in order and keeps one
log of all of them, with exactly `01`'s form:

```{.bash filename="src/run_all.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# run_all.sh: run every numbered step in order; stop at the first failure.
# Run from the project folder:  pixi run bash src/run_all.sh
# Log: logs/run_all_<date>_XXXX.log (01 also keeps its own log)
set -euo pipefail
[[ -f pixi.toml ]] || { echo "run from the project folder" >&2; exit 1; }
mkdir -p logs
log="$(mktemp "logs/run_all_$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M%S)_XXXX.log")"
{
  bash src/01_count_reads.sh
  bash src/02_gtf_summary.sh
} 2>&1 | tee "$log"
```

Because `pipefail` is set inside the script, a failing step makes
`run_all.sh` fail, despite `tee`. (A `| tee` typed in the terminal
around `run_all.sh` would not have `pipefail`, and would bring back the
problem you saw in @sec-shell-scripts-read.) Run the pipeline:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
pixi run bash src/run_all.sh; echo "exit $?"
cat results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv
```

```{.console}
started:  2026-11-22 14:26:49 -0600
host:     your-laptop
script:   f28575917774e7916b14362989eeed68  src/01_count_reads.sh
seqkit:   seqkit v2.14.0
checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: OK
command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz
output:   e1d81de77934f7ab7b44bf72b7520b32  results/read_counts.tsv
finished: 2026-11-22 14:26:50 -0600
[2026-11-22 14:26:50] start; input md5: 504334f6741ee771c665ae845429087f  data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
[2026-11-22 14:26:50] wrote results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv (5 feature types)
[2026-11-22 14:26:50] output md5: 3b9c2b4c499d85a7e70aaf3faaef3c99  results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv
exit 0
feature	count
exon	129
transcript	124
CDS	118
start_codon	115
stop_codon	114
```

The five counts are @sec-text-tools's, now as a two-column table that
other programs can read. `ls logs` shows two new logs, one from `01`
and one from `run_all.sh` holding the whole run. Run from `~`,
`02_gtf_summary.sh` stops with `ERROR: run from the project folder`,
exit status 1.

**A failed rerun.** @sec-shell-scripts-logging promised that a failed
step publishes no new result, but that an older one may still be
there. See it in the scratch copy: give it `02`, the GTF, and the
project's `pixi.toml`, run `02` once, then swap in a damaged GTF (cut
to its first 5,000 bytes, on a copy, as in @sec-getting-help) and run
it again.

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/proj-copy
mkdir -p data/ref
cp ~/bioinf-computing/pixi.toml .
cp ~/bioinf-computing/src/02_gtf_summary.sh src/
cp ~/bioinf-computing/data/ref/genes.gtf.gz data/ref/
bash src/02_gtf_summary.sh; echo "first run exit $?"
md5sum results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv
head -c 5000 ~/bioinf-computing/data/ref/genes.gtf.gz > data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
bash src/02_gtf_summary.sh; echo "rerun exit $?"
md5sum results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv
ls results
cat results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv.tmp
```

(`cp` follows the `data/ref` link of @sec-organizing-projects and
copies the file itself.)

```{.console}
[2026-11-22 14:44:15] start; input md5: 504334f6741ee771c665ae845429087f  data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
[2026-11-22 14:44:15] wrote results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv (5 feature types)
[2026-11-22 14:44:15] output md5: 3b9c2b4c499d85a7e70aaf3faaef3c99  results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv
first run exit 0
3b9c2b4c499d85a7e70aaf3faaef3c99  results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv
[2026-11-22 14:44:17] start; input md5: 7e4688760800a9e5632424a6f67a00ae  data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
gunzip: data/ref/genes.gtf.gz: unexpected end of file
gunzip: data/ref/genes.gtf.gz: uncompress failed
rerun exit 1
3b9c2b4c499d85a7e70aaf3faaef3c99  results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv
gtf_feature_counts.tsv  gtf_feature_counts.tsv.tmp
feature	count
CDS	39
exon	39
start_codon	39
stop_codon	38
transcript	38
```

(Captured on a Mac; GNU gzip says `gzip: data/ref/genes.gtf.gz:
unexpected end of file`.) The rerun logged a different input checksum,
failed with exit status 1, and wrote no `wrote …` line. The old result
is untouched: same checksum. And the leftover `.tmp` holds counts that
**look** like a real result. Had the step written straight to the final
name, that partial table would now be `gtf_feature_counts.tsv`. The
file on disk is the *last good* result, not this run's; the exit status
and the log say which run you are looking at.

**Now name it.** A numbered pipeline is a set of scripts with three
habits (@fig-numbered-pipeline):

- Each step reads only raw inputs or earlier steps' results, and writes
  only its own outputs.
- Each step can be rerun safely: it overwrites its own result, never
  an input (assuming one run at a time).
- The number is the order; the name says what the step does
  (@sec-organizing-projects's naming rule).

`run_all.sh` lists the steps **by name**, not with a pattern such as
`for s in src/[0-9]*.sh`, so a stray `03_old_try.sh` never runs by
accident. The pattern version is shorter, and some people prefer it;
listing by name means you must add each new step to `run_all.sh`
yourself.

::: {#fig-numbered-pipeline}
{{< svg ../figures/numbered-pipeline.svg >}}

The project's numbered pipeline. `run_all.sh` calls `01_count_reads.sh`
(reads in, read counts out, after a checksum check) and then
`02_gtf_summary.sh` (annotation in, feature counts out), stopping at
the first failure; `01` and `run_all.sh` write logs. On the right, what
a workflow manager adds.
:::

**Its limits** are why Part VI exists. A numbered pipeline reruns
every step even when nothing changed; runs one step at a time, even
when two steps could run side by side; cannot resume after a failure
from where it stopped; and does not know which result came from which
version of its inputs. Workflow managers (@sec-workflow-managers) solve
these, as does the older `make` (see the [GNU make
