manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/make/manual/)); nf-core
(@sec-nf-core) is the one you will use. Running each step as a cluster
job is @sec-hpc-slurm.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** You add `03_plot.sh` to `src/` but forget to list
it in `run_all.sh`. What happens when you run the pipeline?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
It never runs, and nothing warns you. Listing steps by name is
deliberate, so check `run_all.sh` whenever you add a step.
:::
:::

## When a script misbehaves {#sec-shell-scripts-debugging}

Two tools find most bugs in short scripts: `bash -x`, which shows each
command as bash runs it, and ShellCheck, which reads a script without
running it. Save this script, which has two bugs from earlier sections,
as `~/bioinf-computing-ch08/broken.sh`:

```{.bash filename="broken.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# broken.sh: count the reads in each R1 file and save the counts.
outdir=~/bioinf-computing-ch08/out
mkdir -p "$outdir"
for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz; do
  n=$(gunzip -c $f | wc -l)
  echo "$f $(( n / 4 ))" >> "$outdri/counts.txt"
done
```

Run it from the practice folder with `bash -x`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
bash -x ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/broken.sh
```

```{.console}
+ outdir=/home/you/bioinf-computing-ch08/out
+ mkdir -p /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch08/out
+ for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz
++ gunzip -c Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
++ wc -l
+ n=0
+ echo 'Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz 0'
/home/you/bioinf-computing-ch08/broken.sh: line 7: /counts.txt: Permission denied
+ for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz
++ gunzip -c run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
++ wc -l
+ n=8
+ echo 'run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz 2'
/home/you/bioinf-computing-ch08/broken.sh: line 7: /counts.txt: Permission denied
…
```

(gunzip's three error lines after `++ wc -l` are left out here.) Each
line starting with `+` is a command after bash has expanded it; `++`
marks a command inside `$( )`. Both bugs are visible. `gunzip -c Run 3
final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz` shows the unquoted `$f` split into three
words (@fig-word-splitting), so sample C counts 0. And
`"$outdri/counts.txt"` became `/counts.txt`: the misspelled variable is
empty, and the write fails only because an ordinary user may not write
to `/`. (On a Mac the message says `Read-only file system` instead.)
`set -x` at the top of a script does the same as `bash -x`, from that
line on.

Now ask ShellCheck, which is in the book environment:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08
pixi run --manifest-path ~/bioinf-computing/pixi.toml shellcheck broken.sh
```

```{.console}
In broken.sh line 6:
  n=$(gunzip -c $f | wc -l)
                ^-- SC2086 (info): Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting.

Did you mean:
  n=$(gunzip -c "$f" | wc -l)


In broken.sh line 7:
  echo "$f $(( n / 4 ))" >> "$outdri/counts.txt"
                             ^-----^ SC2154 (warning): outdri is referenced but not assigned.

For more information:
  https://www.shellcheck.net/wiki/SC2154 -- outdri is referenced but not assi...
  https://www.shellcheck.net/wiki/SC2086 -- Double quote to prevent globbing ...
```

Both bugs are named, with line numbers, before the script ever runs;
ShellCheck exits with status 1 when it finds something. Each code
(`SC2086`) has a page on the [ShellCheck
wiki](https://www.shellcheck.net/wiki/SC2086) that explains why.

If pixi says `shellcheck` is not found, you set up the book environment
before ShellCheck joined it. Download the current environment files
into the project and install them, as in @sec-book-setup:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
curl -fLO {{< var setup-url >}}/pixi.toml
curl -fLO {{< var setup-url >}}/pixi.lock
pixi install --locked
pixi run shellcheck --version
```

The last line should print a version, 0.11.0 or later.

Two more things, one sentence each. The [ShellCheck extension for VS
Code](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=timonwong.shellcheck)
underlines the same problems as you type: search the Extensions view
for its ID, `timonwong.shellcheck`; it needs no further setup, and
hovering over the underlined `$f` shows the same SC2086 message. And
the Mac's own `/bin/bash` is version 3.2, which lacks features such as
`mapfile`, `declare -A`, and `${x,,}` (`mapfile: command not found`):
`#!/usr/bin/env bash`, with @sec-orientation's current bash, avoids
it. Debuggers, tests, and linting in depth are @sec-reusable-code.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Tip
Run ShellCheck on every script before you trust it, and keep the VS
Code extension on while you write.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** ShellCheck says `SC2086: Double quote to prevent
globbing and word splitting` on `gunzip -c $f`. Which rule of this
chapter is it, and what is the fix?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Quote every expansion (@sec-shell-scripts-variables): `gunzip -c
"$f"`, so a name with spaces stays one argument.
:::
:::

## Saving scripts with git {#sec-shell-scripts-git}

Your project now has three scripts that work. Before you change them
again, save this working state so you can always get it back. git keeps
a history of your files; this section uses a five-command routine, and
@sec-git teaches git properly, starting from this repository.

**One-time setup.** Check that git is installed. On a Mac it came with
the Xcode Command Line Tools that Homebrew installed in
@sec-orientation; Ubuntu, WSL, and clusters have it already:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
git --version
```

```{.console}
git version 2.50.1 (Apple Git-155)
```

You need git 2.28 or later for the setup shown here (`git restore`
itself needs 2.23, and the `init.defaultBranch` setting below arrived
in 2.28); every system checked for this book had a newer one. Then tell git your name and
email (they are stored in each commit) and the name for the first
branch, **before** making a repository:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.org"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

Without the last line, `git init` prints several lines of `hint:`
about the default branch name, worded differently in different git
versions. They are harmless; the setting just makes the name `main`
and stops the hint.

**Tell git what not to save.** In `~/bioinf-computing`, make a file
`.gitignore` (`code .gitignore`), paste, and save:

```{.default filename=".gitignore"}
data/
results/
logs/
.pixi/
```

Each line is a folder git will ignore: `data/` because the raw data are
large, read-only, and backed up elsewhere (@sec-organizing-projects);
`results/` and `logs/` because the scripts rebuild them; `.pixi/`
because `pixi install --locked` rebuilds the environment from
`pixi.lock`. @sec-git covers `.gitignore` rules in full.

**The routine.** Make the project a repository, look, add, commit, and
look at the history:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
git init
git status --short
git add .gitignore src/ README.md NOTEBOOK.md pixi.toml pixi.lock
git status --short
git commit -m "Add read-count and GTF summary scripts"
git log --oneline
```

```{.console}
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/you/bioinf-computing/.git/
?? .gitignore
?? NOTEBOOK.md
?? README.md
?? pixi.lock
?? pixi.toml
?? src/
A  .gitignore
A  NOTEBOOK.md
A  README.md
A  pixi.lock
A  pixi.toml
A  src/01_count_reads.sh
A  src/02_gtf_summary.sh
A  src/run_all.sh
[main (root-commit) 447c010] Add read-count and GTF summary scripts
 8 files changed, 4605 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
 …
447c010 Add read-count and GTF summary scripts
```

(Your commit IDs, such as `447c010`, will differ, and `git status` may
list other files you made, such as `notes.txt`.) `??` means "not yet
tracked"; `A` means "added, ready to commit". `data/`, `results/`,
`logs/`, and `.pixi/` never appear: `.gitignore` works.

**Break it.** Make a mistake on purpose, comment out the strict-mode
line, and see what git shows:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
sed -i 's/^set -euo pipefail$/# set -euo pipefail/' src/01_count_reads.sh
git status --short
git diff
```

```{.console}
 M src/01_count_reads.sh
diff --git a/src/01_count_reads.sh b/src/01_count_reads.sh
index 5b963b8..05e986d 100644
--- a/src/01_count_reads.sh
+++ b/src/01_count_reads.sh
@@ -1,7 +1,7 @@
 #!/usr/bin/env bash
 # 01_count_reads.sh: check the raw FASTQ files, then count their reads.
 # Run from the project folder:  pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh
-set -euo pipefail
+# set -euo pipefail
 [[ -f pixi.toml ]] || { echo "run from the project folder" >&2; exit 1; }

 mkdir -p results logs
```

` M` means "modified since the last commit". `git diff` shows the
change: `-` for the old line, `+` for the new one. **Read the diff
before you throw anything away.** Then bring the file back:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
git restore src/01_count_reads.sh
git status --short
```

`git status --short` now prints nothing: the file is as it was.
Strictly, `git restore file` copies the **staged** version of the file
(the one your last `git add` recorded), which here is the same as the
last commit because nothing was staged since; @sec-git explains the
staging area.

**Get back an older version.** Make a small second change and commit
it, so there are two commits. For example, in `src/02_gtf_summary.sh`
change the `# Output:` comment to read `(two columns: feature, count;
most common first)`, then:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
git add src/02_gtf_summary.sh
git commit -m "Describe the output columns of 02"
git log --oneline
git show --stat HEAD
```

```{.console}
[main 71bad40] Describe the output columns of 02
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
71bad40 Describe the output columns of 02
447c010 Add read-count and GTF summary scripts
…
 src/02_gtf_summary.sh | 2 +-
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
```

`git log --oneline` shows only the messages; `git show --stat HEAD`
shows which files the latest commit (`HEAD`) changed. Now suppose the
older version was better. `HEAD~1` means "one commit before the
latest". Look at the old file, bring it back, check it, and save the
recovery as a new commit:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
git show HEAD~1:src/02_gtf_summary.sh | head -n 5
git restore --source=HEAD~1 src/02_gtf_summary.sh
git status --short
pixi run bash src/run_all.sh
git commit -am "Restore the shorter output comment in 02"
git log --oneline
```

```{.console}
…
# Output: results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv (feature, count; most common first)
 M src/02_gtf_summary.sh
…
947b2e9 Restore the shorter output comment in 02
71bad40 Describe the output columns of 02
447c010 Add read-count and GTF summary scripts
```

Nothing was lost: the history still holds all three versions
(@fig-git-routine). `git commit -am` adds every changed tracked file
and commits in one step.

::: {#fig-git-routine}
{{< svg ../figures/git-routine.svg >}}

The minimal git routine. Your files are changed in the working folder,
staged with `git add`, and saved in the history with `git commit`.
`git status` and `git diff` look at what changed. `git restore file`
brings back the staged copy (normally the last commit, here), and `git
restore --source=HEAD~1 file` brings back a file from an older commit.
:::

**Now name it.** A commit is a saved snapshot of the files you added,
with a message saying why. Here git does not save `data/` or
`results/`, by design. The habit: commit each time a script works, and
before you change it. VS Code shows the same information in its
[Source Control
view](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/sourcecontrol/overview).
Everything else, such as branches, undoing commits, and remotes, is
@sec-git. @tbl-git-routine lists the routine.

: The minimal git routine. {#tbl-git-routine}

| When | Command | What it does |
|:-----|:--------|:-------------|
| Once per computer | `git config --global user.name …`, `user.email …`, `init.defaultBranch main` | who you are; name of the first branch |
| Once per project | `git init` | make the folder a repository |
| Every change | `git status --short`, `git diff` | what changed, line by line |
| | `git add file`, `git commit -m "why"` | stage the change, save a snapshot |
| Look back | `git log --oneline`, `git show --stat HEAD`, `git show HEAD~1:file` | the history; files in a commit; an old version |
| Undo an edit | `git restore file` | back to the staged copy (normally the last commit) |
| Bring back an old version | `git restore --source=HEAD~1 file` | the file as it was one commit ago |
| Everything else | branches, undoing commits, remotes | @sec-git |

::: {.callout-note}
## Background
git stores the files you add, as they were at each commit. It does not
store what `.gitignore` excludes: here, data and results, by design.
And a repository on the same disk is not an off-machine backup: if the
disk fails, the `.git/` folder goes with it. Pushing to another machine
is one way to make an independent copy (@sec-github).
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** You edited `02_gtf_summary.sh`, it broke, and you
have not committed or staged the change. How do you get the last
working version back?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Look at the change first with `git diff`, then `git restore
src/02_gtf_summary.sh`, and check with `git status --short`. It brings
back the staged copy, which is the last commit when nothing was
staged.
:::
:::

## Summary {#sec-shell-scripts-summary}

- A script is commands saved in a file and run, top to bottom, by a new
  bash process. Start it with `#!/usr/bin/env bash` and a header comment
  that says what it does, how to run it, and what it reads and writes.
  Relative paths are read from where it is **run**, so project scripts
  are run from the project folder.
- `$name` is replaced by its value; unquoted, that value is split at
  spaces and matched as a wildcard. Put double quotes around every
  expansion: `"$f"`, `"$@"`, `"${sample}_R1.fastq.gz"`. `$( )` captures a
  command's output and `$(( ))` does whole-number arithmetic.
- Loop over a glob, never over `ls` or `$(cat file)`; read table rows
  with `while IFS=$'\t' read -r`. Preview a loop with `echo` before it
  changes anything, and check that a list of files is not empty.
- `if` tests an exit status; `[[ ]]` tests files, text, and numbers
  (`<` compares text, `-lt` and `(( ))` compare numbers). Take file names
  as arguments with `"$@"`, and stop with a usage message (exit 2) when
  they are missing. `set -euo pipefail` stops on a reported failure, an
  unset variable, or a failed pipe stage; it cannot see a tool that
  reports success on bad input, so check results too.
- Send results to stdout and messages to stderr, and keep a log of each
  run. Write each output to `name.tmp` and `mv` it into place only after
  the step succeeds. Numbered scripts run in order by `run_all.sh` make
  a small pipeline. Commit each script once it works, look with
  `git status` and `git diff`, and bring back an old version with
  `git restore`.

A template to start every script from. Delete the lines you do not
need; keep `set -euo pipefail`.

```{.bash filename="template.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# NAME.sh: what this script does, in one line.
# Run:    bash NAME.sh FILE [MORE ...]   (from the project folder)
# Input:  what it reads
# Output: what it writes (results on stdout or in results/, messages on stderr)
set -euo pipefail
shopt -s nullglob     # only if the script loops over a glob

log() { printf '[%s] %s\n' "$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')" "$*" >&2; }
die() { log "ERROR: $*"; exit 1; }

if [[ $# -lt 1 ]]; then
  echo "usage: NAME.sh FILE [MORE ...]" >&2
  exit 2
fi

out="results/NAME.tsv"
mkdir -p results
log "start"
for f in "$@"; do
  [[ -s "$f" ]] || die "missing or empty: $f"
  printf '%s\t%s\n' "$(basename "$f")" "something about $f"
done > "$out.tmp"
mv "$out.tmp" "$out"
log "wrote $out"
```

@tbl-ch08-commands collects the chapter's commands.

: The chapter's commands on one page. {#tbl-ch08-commands}

| Task | Command |
|:-----|:--------|
| Run a script | `bash script.sh`, or `chmod u+x script.sh` then `./script.sh` |
| Variables | `name=value` (no spaces), `"$name"`, `"${name}_R1.fastq.gz"` |
| Capture output, do arithmetic | `n=$(wc -l < "$f")`, `$(( n / 4 ))` |
| Trim a value | `${f##*/}` (drop folders), `${f%.gz}` (drop an ending), `basename "$f"` |
| Lists | `files=(*.fastq.gz)`, `"${files[@]}"`, `${#files[@]}` |
| Loops | `for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz; do …; done`, `for i in {01..03}`, `while IFS=$'\t' read -r a b c; do …; done < table.tsv` |
| Tests | `if [[ -s "$f" ]]; then …; fi`, `[[ "$a" == "$b" ]]`, `(( n > 0 ))` |
| Arguments | `"$1"`, `"$@"`, `$#`, `$0`; usage message with `>&2` and `exit 2` |
| Stop on errors | `set -euo pipefail`; inspect a pipe with `"${PIPESTATUS[@]}"` |
| Logging | `> results.tsv 2> run.log`, `{ …; } 2>&1 \| tee "$log"`, `mktemp` |
| Safe output | `cmd > "$out.tmp"` then `mv "$out.tmp" "$out"` |
| Find bugs | `bash -x script.sh`, `pixi run shellcheck script.sh` |
| git routine | `git status`, `git diff`, `git add`, `git commit -m "…"`, `git log --oneline`, `git show --stat HEAD`, `git restore file`, `git restore --source=HEAD~1 file` |

**Exercise 1. Finish `count_reads.sh`.** Part A after
@sec-shell-scripts-arguments; part B after @sec-shell-scripts-strict.

A labmate's script counts the reads in each FASTQ file it is given.
Save it as `~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh` (`code
~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh`, paste, save) and make it
executable with `chmod u+x ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh`:

```{.bash filename="~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count_reads.sh: print each FASTQ file's name and its number of reads.
# Usage: count_reads.sh FILE.fastq.gz [MORE.fastq.gz ...]
for f in $@; do
  n=$(gunzip -c $f | wc -l)
  echo "$f $((n / 4))"
done
```

Run it from the practice folder on every R1 file, and on a file that
does not exist:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh */*_R1*; echo "exit $?"
~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh missing.fastq.gz; echo "exit $?"
```

Write down what is wrong. Then fix it one change at a time, rerunning
after each, and record each change in `NOTEBOOK.md`.

- **Part A.** Quote `"$@"` and `"$f"`. Add a usage check that prints
  `usage: count_reads.sh FILE.fastq.gz [MORE.fastq.gz ...]` to stderr
  and exits 2 when there are no arguments. Print the file's base name
  and its count separated by a tab. Run it with the tighter pattern
  `*/*_R1.f*q.gz`.
- **Part B.** Add `set -euo pipefail` and run the missing file again.
  What changed, and why?

The goal, from `~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share`:

```{.console}
$ ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh */*_R1.f*q.gz
sample_C_R1.fq.gz	4
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz	2
sample_B_R1.fastq.gz	3
```

and two runs that stop with a message and a nonzero status, printing no
count: no arguments (exit 2) and a missing file (exit 1).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

The script as supplied (captured on macOS; on Linux, GNU gzip words
each error as `gzip: Run.gz: No such file or directory`):

```{.console}
$ ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh */*_R1*; echo "exit $?"
gunzip: can't stat: Run (Run.gz): No such file or directory
Run 0
gunzip: can't stat: 3 (3.gz): No such file or directory
3 0
gunzip: can't stat: final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz (final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz.gz): No such file or directory
final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz 0
run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz 2
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz 3
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp 3
exit 0
```

Three faults, and the status says 0 through all of them. The unquoted
`$@` and `$f` split `Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz` into three names
(@sec-shell-scripts-variables), so sample C counts as `0` three times.
The pattern `*_R1*` also matched the stray `.tmp` copy, counted as a
fourth sample (@sec-shell-scripts-loops). The missing file prints an
error, then `missing.fastq.gz 0`, and still exits 0.

The finished script:

```{.bash filename="~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count_reads.sh: print each FASTQ file's name and its number of reads.
# Usage: count_reads.sh FILE.fastq.gz [MORE.fastq.gz ...]
set -euo pipefail

if [[ $# -lt 1 ]]; then
  echo "usage: count_reads.sh FILE.fastq.gz [MORE.fastq.gz ...]" >&2
  exit 2
fi

for f in "$@"; do
  n=$(gunzip -c "$f" | wc -l)
  printf '%s\t%s\n' "$(basename "$f")" "$((n / 4))"
done
```

```{.console}
$ ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh */*_R1.f*q.gz; echo "exit $?"
sample_C_R1.fq.gz	4
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz	2
sample_B_R1.fastq.gz	3
exit 0
$ ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh; echo "exit $?"
usage: count_reads.sh FILE.fastq.gz [MORE.fastq.gz ...]
exit 2
$ ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh missing.fastq.gz; echo "exit $?"
gzip: missing.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
exit 1
```

After part A alone the missing file still printed `missing.fastq.gz`, a
tab, and `0`, with exit 0: quoting and the usage check do not stop a
failed `gunzip`. Part B's `set -euo pipefail` does. `pipefail` makes
the `gunzip | wc -l` pipeline fail when `gunzip` fails, and `-e` stops
the script at that line, before it prints a count. (On a Mac, Apple
gzip words the error `gunzip: can't stat: missing.fastq.gz …`.)

The order of the three lines comes from bash's sort of the matched
names, which depends on your locale: here `Run 3 final` sorts first,
but on many Linux clusters it comes last. The counts are what matter.
`pixi run shellcheck count_reads.sh` on the supplied version flags the
unquoted `$@` (SC2068) and `$f` (SC2086); on the finished one it prints
nothing.
:::
:::

**Exercise 2. Check a sample table against the disk.** After
@sec-shell-scripts-strict.

The sample table `meta/samples.tsv` lists a run folder for each
sample. Save this script as `~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/check_samples.sh`.
It is the loop from @sec-shell-scripts-loops that reads the table with
`<` instead of a pipe, so the `bad` flag survives the loop:

```{.bash filename="~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/check_samples.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# check_samples.sh: check that each sample in a table has its run folder.
# Usage:  check_samples.sh TABLE
#   TABLE: tab-separated, header line first, columns sample, run_folder, ...
#   Run it from the folder that the run_folder paths are relative to.
# Problems go to stderr; exit 1 if any row has a problem.
set -euo pipefail

if [[ $# -ne 1 ]]; then
  echo "usage: check_samples.sh TABLE" >&2
  exit 2
fi
table="$1"
[[ -r "$table" ]] || { echo "cannot read: $table" >&2; exit 1; }

bad=0
{
  IFS= read -r _   # skip the header line
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r sample folder rest || [[ -n "$sample$folder$rest" ]]; do
    if [[ ! -d "$folder" ]]; then
      printf '%s: missing folder %s\n' "$sample" "$folder" >&2
      bad=1
    fi
    # Your turn: when the folder exists, check that it holds an R1 file
    # for this sample (sample_X_R1.fastq.gz or .fq.gz), and report it if not.
  done
} < "$table"
exit "$bad"
```

Run it from `~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share` with `bash
~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/check_samples.sh meta/samples.tsv; echo
"exit $?"`. It already reports missing folders on stderr, keeps going
after a bad row, and exits 1 if any row failed. Add the R1 check: when
the folder exists, look for that sample's R1 file, report it the same
way if there is none, and print the sample and its R1 file, separated
by a tab, on stdout when there is one.

Then a prediction. Make a copy, `check_samples_csv.sh`, that reads
`meta/samples_from_excel.csv` with `IFS=,`, keeps the last column (`read -r sample folder _ reads ||
[[ -n "$sample$folder$reads" ]]`),
and also checks that `reads` is a positive number with `if ! (( reads >
0 ))`. Before running it: which checks will pass, and which will fail?
Run it and explain the result from @sec-linux-system-line-endings.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

Add `shopt -s nullglob` under `set -euo pipefail`, so a pattern that
matches nothing gives an empty list, and replace the `fi` and the
comment with an `else` branch:

```{.bash filename="~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/check_samples.sh (the loop)"}
    if [[ ! -d "$folder" ]]; then
      printf '%s: missing folder %s\n' "$sample" "$folder" >&2
      bad=1
    else
      r1=("$folder/${sample}"_R1.f*q.gz)
      if (( ${#r1[@]} == 0 )); then
        printf '%s: no R1 file in %s\n' "$sample" "$folder" >&2
        bad=1
      else
        printf '%s\t%s\n' "$sample" "${r1[0]}"
      fi
    fi
```

```{.console}
$ bash ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/check_samples.sh meta/samples.tsv; echo "exit $?"
sample_C	Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
sample_A	run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
sample_B	run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
sample_E: missing folder run5
sample_B	run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
sample_D: missing folder run4
exit 1
```

With `2>/dev/null` only the four found rows remain: results and
problems go to different streams (@sec-shell-scripts-logging). Every
bad row is reported, not just the first. To see the R1 check fire, copy
the table to `~/bioinf-computing-ch08/`, add a row `sample_Z`, tab,
`run1`, and run on the copy: the output gains `sample_Z: no R1 file in
run1`. The supplied version printed only the two `missing folder` lines.
A follow-up worth thinking about: `sample_B` is listed twice. The table
has a duplicate row, which this script does not look for.

The CSV copy (captured with bash 5.3):

```{.console}
$ bash ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/check_samples_csv.sh meta/samples_from_excel.csv
…check_samples_csv.sh: line 22: ((: 12: arithmetic syntax error: invalid arithmetic operator (error token is "")
sample_C: reads is not a positive number: 12
sample_C	Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
…
```

Every row fails the number test, and the message even says `12` is not
a positive number. The folder and R1 checks give the same result as the
TSV. The file has Windows line endings, so each line's **last** field,
`reads`, ends in an invisible `\r`: `12\r` is not a number, but the
`\r` does not show on screen. The folder name is not the last field, so
those checks never notice. After `tr -d '\r' < meta/samples_from_excel.csv
> samples_lf.csv`, the copy run on `samples_lf.csv` gives the TSV's
result. The error does not stop the script, because it sits in an `if`.
Older bash versions, such as 5.1 on many clusters, word the message
differently. `IFS=,` works for this simple file only; a real CSV reader
handles quoted commas (@sec-tabular-data).
:::
:::

**Exercise 3. What strict mode misses.** After @sec-shell-scripts-strict.

Save this script as `~/bioinf-computing-ch08/ex3/count_ok.sh`:

```{.bash filename="~/bioinf-computing-ch08/ex3/count_ok.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count_ok.sh: count the reads in one FASTQ file, then report OK.
# Usage: count_ok.sh FILE.fastq.gz
n=$(gunzip -c "$1" | wc -l)
echo "$(basename "$1"): $((n / 4)) reads"
echo "OK"
```

Make a good input and three bad ones next to it: a truncated copy, and
a gzip file that is valid but holds nothing (`missing.fastq.gz` you do
not make at all):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/ex3
cp ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz good.fastq.gz
head -c 30 good.fastq.gz > trunc.fastq.gz
gzip < /dev/null > empty.fastq.gz
for f in good missing trunc empty; do bash count_ok.sh "$f.fastq.gz"; echo "exit $?"; done
```

All four end with `OK` and exit 0. Add `set -euo pipefail` and predict
which inputs it stops before you rerun. Then add **one** explicit check
so that the remaining bad input stops the script with a message on
stderr and exit 1, while `good.fastq.gz` still prints `3 reads` and
`OK`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

With `set -euo pipefail` (GNU gzip wording):

```{.console}
$ for f in good missing trunc empty; do bash count_ok.sh "$f.fastq.gz"; echo "exit $?"; done
good.fastq.gz: 3 reads
OK
exit 0
gzip: missing.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
exit 1
gzip: trunc.fastq.gz: unexpected end of file
exit 1
empty.fastq.gz: 0 reads
OK
exit 0
```

Strict mode catches the missing and the truncated file, because
`gunzip` reports both as failures and `pipefail` passes that on. (Apple
gzip words them `gunzip: can't stat: …` and `gunzip: trunc.fastq.gz:
unexpected end of file`.) The empty file is a **valid** gzip stream with
no content: `gunzip` succeeds, `wc -l` prints `0`, and nothing has
reported a failure. Only a check of the result catches it:

```{.bash filename="~/bioinf-computing-ch08/ex3/count_ok.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count_ok.sh: count the reads in one FASTQ file, then report OK.
# Usage: count_ok.sh FILE.fastq.gz
set -euo pipefail
if [[ $# -ne 1 ]]; then echo "usage: count_ok.sh FILE.fastq.gz" >&2; exit 2; fi

n=$(gunzip -c "$1" | wc -l)
reads=$((n / 4))
if (( reads == 0 )); then
  echo "$(basename "$1"): no reads" >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "$(basename "$1"): $reads reads"
echo "OK"
```

```{.console}
$ bash count_ok.sh empty.fastq.gz; echo "exit $?"
empty.fastq.gz: no reads
exit 1
$ bash count_ok.sh good.fastq.gz; echo "exit $?"
good.fastq.gz: 3 reads
OK
exit 0
```

The other checks you might reach for do not work here. `gzip -t
empty.fastq.gz` exits 0, because the stream is valid, and `[[ -s
empty.fastq.gz ]]` is true, because the file holds 20 bytes of gzip
header. Do not confuse it with a zero-byte file named `.gz`, which
`gunzip` and `gzip -t` both reject. Dividing lines by 4 is right only
for these plain four-line toy records; it does not check that a file is
valid FASTQ. Tools that read the format properly come in
@sec-fasta-fastq.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 4. Add a third step to the project.** After
@sec-shell-scripts-pipeline.

Add `src/03_transcript_biotypes.sh`, which counts the transcripts of
each biotype (protein-coding, tRNA, and so on) in the reference
annotation and writes `results/transcript_biotypes.tsv`. Follow
`02_gtf_summary.sh`: header comment, `set -euo pipefail`, the
project-folder guard, `log` and `die`, an input check, the `.tmp` and
`mv`, and the two MD5 log lines. One line is new to you (`grep -o`
prints only the part of each line that matches), so here it is:

```{.bash filename="the extraction line for src/03_transcript_biotypes.sh"}
gunzip -c "$gtf" | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "transcript"' \
  | grep -o 'transcript_biotype "[^"]*"' | cut -d'"' -f2 \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr | awk -v OFS='\t' '{print $2, $1}'
```

Add the step to `run_all.sh`, run the whole pipeline with `pixi run bash
src/run_all.sh`, and check that the counts add up to the 124
transcripts of @sec-text-tools. Commit the new script and the changed
`run_all.sh` with a message that says what the step does, and check
the commit with `git show --stat HEAD`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

```{.bash filename="src/03_transcript_biotypes.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# 03_transcript_biotypes.sh: count transcripts of each biotype in the reference annotation.
# Run from the project folder:  pixi run bash src/03_transcript_biotypes.sh
# Input:  data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
# Output: results/transcript_biotypes.tsv (biotype, count; most common first)
set -euo pipefail

log() { printf '[%s] %s\n' "$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')" "$*" >&2; }
die() { log "ERROR: $*"; exit 1; }

[[ -f pixi.toml ]] || die "run from the project folder"

gtf="data/ref/genes.gtf.gz"
out="results/transcript_biotypes.tsv"
[[ -s "$gtf" ]] || die "missing or empty: $gtf"

mkdir -p results
log "start; input md5: $(md5sum "$gtf")"
{
  printf 'biotype\tcount\n'
  gunzip -c "$gtf" | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "transcript"' \
    | grep -o 'transcript_biotype "[^"]*"' | cut -d'"' -f2 \
    | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr | awk -v OFS='\t' '{print $2, $1}'
} > "$out.tmp"
mv "$out.tmp" "$out"
log "wrote $out ($(( $(wc -l < "$out") - 1 )) biotypes)"
log "output md5: $(md5sum "$out")"
```

In `run_all.sh`, add `bash src/03_transcript_biotypes.sh` after the
`02` line, inside the `{ … }` group. The new step's log lines and
result:

```{.console}
[2026-11-22 15:08:39] start; input md5: 504334f6741ee771c665ae845429087f  data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
[2026-11-22 15:08:39] wrote results/transcript_biotypes.tsv (5 biotypes)
[2026-11-22 15:08:40] output md5: 06f05e65e07083ae63267ee916dedccc  results/transcript_biotypes.tsv
$ cat results/transcript_biotypes.tsv
biotype	count
protein_coding	116
tRNA	4
pseudogene	2
ncRNA	1
snoRNA	1
```

116 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 124, the transcript count from
`gtf_feature_counts.tsv`. Your MD5 should match: the tied `ncRNA` and
`snoRNA` rows come out in the same order whatever your locale. Then:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
git add src/03_transcript_biotypes.sh src/run_all.sh
git commit -m "Add step 03: count transcripts by biotype"
git show --stat HEAD
```

`git show --stat HEAD` lists both files. One more thing to notice:
`02` and `03` both read only the GTF and write different files, so
they could run at the same time. `run_all.sh` runs them one after the
other, one of the limits in @sec-shell-scripts-pipeline that workflow
managers remove.
:::
:::

**Exercise 5. Break, see, recover.** After @sec-shell-scripts-git.

In `~/bioinf-computing`, delete the line that prints the header in
`src/02_gtf_summary.sh` (`printf 'feature\tcount\n'`), run the script,
and commit the change as if you had not noticed. Then find what
changed, bring back the working version from the commit before, check
that it works, and commit the recovery. Record each command and what it
showed in `NOTEBOOK.md`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

The broken script still runs and exits 0, but its log says `wrote
results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv (4 feature types)`, and the file starts
with `exon	129`: the header is gone, and the count of "feature types"
is now one short because the script subtracts a header line that is
not there. Nothing failed; only reading the result shows the problem.

```{.console}
$ git commit -am "Drop header line from GTF summary"
$ git log --oneline -- src/02_gtf_summary.sh
<hash> Drop header line from GTF summary
<hash> Add read-count and GTF summary scripts
$ git diff HEAD~1
diff --git a/src/02_gtf_summary.sh b/src/02_gtf_summary.sh
…
 {
-  printf 'feature\tcount\n'
   gunzip -c "$gtf" | cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr \
     | awk -v OFS='\t' '{print $2, $1}'
 } > "$out.tmp"
$ git restore --source=HEAD~1 src/02_gtf_summary.sh
$ git status --short
 M src/02_gtf_summary.sh
$ pixi run bash src/run_all.sh
$ git commit -am "Restore header line in GTF summary"
```

Your commit hashes (shown as `<hash>`) and messages will differ, and
your history may have more commits. `git log -- file` lists only the commits that changed that
file. `git diff HEAD~1` compares your files with the commit before the
last one, so the removed line shows with a `-`. `git restore
--source=HEAD~1` copies the file as it was in that commit into your
folder; `git status` shows it as modified, because it now differs from
the last commit. Rerunning `run_all.sh` should give five feature types
again, and the new commit records the repair without erasing the
mistake from history. (If you had not committed the bad change, `git
restore src/02_gtf_summary.sh` alone would have been enough.)
:::
:::

## Further reading {#sec-shell-scripts-reading}

- @shotts2025linux, *The Linux Command Line*, Part 4 "Writing Shell
  Scripts" --- variables, `if`, loops, and positional parameters, one
  chapter each, in the same order as this chapter; free online.
- @wilson2019swcarpentry, *The Unix Shell*, episodes "Loops" and "Shell
  Scripts" --- a second, shorter walk through the same ideas, with
  exercises and a different dataset.
- @buffalo2015bioinformatics, *Bioinformatics Data Skills*, chapter 12
  "Bioinformatics Shell Scripting, Writing Pipelines, and Parallelizing
  Tasks" --- written for the same readers: `set -euo pipefail`, loops
  over samples, and `make` for pipelines.
- @wilson2017good, "Good enough practices in scientific computing" ---
  the sections on software and project organisation give the reasons
  behind numbered scripts, one command to rerun everything, and version
  control.
- @ramey2025bash, the [*Bash Reference
  Manual*](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/), sections *Shell
  Expansions* and *The Set Builtin* --- the exact rules for word
  splitting and for when `set -e` does and does not stop a script.
  Short, precise, and the place to settle an argument.
